Vier Dialoge (four dialogues, using everything above)

Dialog 1 — Kennenlernen (getting to know each other — formal)
👩‍🏫 Frau Bauer
Guten Tag! Wo wohnen Sie?Good day! Where do you live?
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Ich wohne in Mirpur-khas.I live in Mirpur-khas.
👩‍🏫 Frau Bauer
Sprechen Sie Italienisch?Do you speak Italian?
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Nein, ich verstehe nicht.No, I don't understand.
👩‍🏫 Frau Bauer
Kein Problem! Haben Sie Zeit?No problem! Do you have time?
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Ja, kein Problem.Yes, no problem.

Drills the formal Sie register throughout, plus the V-S-O question pattern in 'Sprechen Sie...?' and 'Haben Sie...?', alongside two rescue phrases.

Dialog 2 — Woher kommst du? (where are you from? — informal)
🙋‍♀️ Ayesha
Hallo! Woher kommst du?Hi! Where are you from?
🙋‍♀️ Sara
Ich komme aus Pakistan.I'm from Pakistan.
🙋‍♀️ Ayesha
Ich wohne in Mirpur. Und du?I live in Mirpur. And you?
🙋‍♀️ Sara
Ich wohne auch in Mirpur!I live in Mirpur too!

Uses the informal du with 'Woher kommst du?' — same question logic as the Sie-questions in Dialogue 1, but a different pronoun register for a friend instead of a stranger.

Dialog 3 — Wir zählen zusammen (counting together)
Ayesha and Sara count together for a clapping game.
🙋‍♀️ Ayesha
Eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf...One, two, three, four, five...
🙋‍♀️ Sara
Sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn!Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!
🙋‍♀️ Ayesha
Elf, zwölf, dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn...Eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen...
🙋‍♀️ Sara
Sechzehn, siebzehn, achtzehn, neunzehn, zwanzig!Sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty!
🙋‍♀️ Ayesha
Kein Problem!No problem!

Runs through all twenty numbers in order and closes with 'kein Problem' as a casual, natural sign-off.

Dialog 4 — Bei der Anmeldung (at the school registration desk)
👩‍💼 Sekretärin
Sind Sie 30 Jahre alt?Are you 30 years old?
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Nein!No!
👩‍💼 Sekretärin
Haben Sie Zeit?Do you have time?
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Ja, kein Problem.Yes, no problem.
👩‍💼 Sekretärin
Verstehen Sie mich?Do you understand me?
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Ja, ich verstehe.Yes, I understand.

Chains three V-S-O yes/no questions back to back (Sind Sie...? Haben Sie...? Verstehen Sie...?) — exactly the rapid-fire pattern likely to show up on tomorrow's test.

Nomen aus dieser Lektion (nouns hiding inside this lesson's phrases)

  • ⏳der Moment / die Momentemoment · Einen Moment, bitte.
  • ⚠️das Problem / die Problemeproblem · Kein Problem.
  • 🤔die Ahnung / die Ahnungenidea, notion · Keine Ahnung.
  • ⏰die Zeit / die Zeitentime · Haben Sie Zeit?
  • 📅das Jahr / die Jahreyear · 30 Jahre alt
  • ⚽der Fußball / die Fußbällefootball, soccer · Spielen Sie Fußball?

These nouns are hiding inside phrases you already learned above — pull them out, learn the article and plural separately, and they become flashcard material too.

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · Ja/Nein-Frage: Verb + Subjekt + Objekt (yes/no question: verb + subject + object)
SpielenVerb · verb, position 1SieSubjekt · subject, formal youFußball?Objekt · object, Akkusativ

The verb leaves its normal spot and leads the sentence. This move marks a yes/no question and tells the listener to answer with ja, nein, or perhaps vielleicht, exactly as in Sprechen Sie Italienisch? and Haben Sie Zeit?

2 · Aussage zum Vergleich: Subjekt + Verb + Rest (statement for comparison: subject + verb + the rest)
IchSubjekt · subjectwohneVerb · verb, position 2in Mirpur-khas.Ort · place

This neutral statement keeps the verb in position 2 and puts the subject in position 1. Ich heiße Priyanka works the same way. This is the shape every Ja/Nein-Frage is built by changing.

3 · Formelle W-Frage: W-Wort + Verb + Sie (formal W-question: question word + verb + formal you)
WoW-Wort · question wordwohnenVerb · verb, position 2Sie?Subjekt · subject, formal

A question word takes position 1 instead of the verb, but the verb still sits in position 2 — the subject follows the verb. Compare this to the Ja/Nein-Frage above, which has no W-Wort at all.

4 · Informelle W-Frage: dieselbe Form, anderes Pronomen (informal W-question: same form, different pronoun)
WoherW-Wort · question wordkommstVerb · verb, position 2du?Subjekt · subject, informal

Identical skeleton to pattern 3 — only Sie becomes du, and the verb ending shifts from -en to -st to match it (Lektion pattern: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t).

5 · haben und sein sind auch V-S-O in der Frage (haben and sein also use V-S-O in questions)
HabenVerb · verb, unregelmäßig (irregular)SieSubjekt · subjectZeit?Objekt · object, Akkusativ
SindVerb · verb, unregelmäßig (irregular)SieSubjekt · subject30 Jahre alt?Rest · the rest: Zahl (number) + Adjektiv (adjective)

Even irregular verbs (haben → habe, hast, hat, haben, habt, haben; sein → bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind) obey the same V-S-O rule for questions — the pattern doesn't care whether the verb is regular.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • Sie (formal you) vs. du (informal you) — Gedächtnisstütze (memory aid): Sie has a big capital S — a big, serious "you" for teachers, elders, and strangers, exactly like آپ rather than تم in Urdu. du is short and small, just like the closeness it names — friends, family, other teens, the تم of German.
  • dreizehn → neunzehn (thirteen to nineteen): dreizehn through neunzehn are just the digit with -zehn ("ten") tacked on — say the digit, then add "-zehn" the way English adds "-teen".
  • zwanzig (twenty) stands alone: Twenty refuses to be "zwei-zehn" — picture it standing apart from the whole 13–19 family, proudly its own word.
  • sechzehn / siebzehn (sixteen / seventeen) lose a letter: sechs and sieben get lazy before -zehn and drop a letter (sechzehn, not sechszehn) — sounds get smoothed out, just like contractions in spoken Urdu.
  • Ich verstehe nicht vs. Ich weiß nicht (I don't understand vs. I don't know): Ich verstehe nicht is about comprehension — you didn't catch the language. Ich weiß nicht is about knowledge — you don't know the fact. Didn't catch it? verstehe nicht. Don't know the answer? weiß nicht.
  • V-S-O announces a Ja/Nein-Frage (yes/no question): the verb sprints to the front whenever a question wants ja or nein — Spielen Sie…? announces "this is a question!" before the subject even shows up.
  • Keine Ahnung (no idea): Ahnung sounds like "a hunch" — keine Ahnung means not even a hunch, no idea at all. Casual — save it for friends, not a teacher.
  • wohnen → wohn + en (to live: stem + ending), and eight more in the present tense: peel off the -en to find the stem (wohn-), then glue on the right ending for each person. The same present-tense ending pattern appears in all nine paradigms in this section: machen, spielen, studieren, kommen, hören, lernen, sagen, gehen.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • Sie spielen Fußball? (statement order + question mark) → Spielen Sie Fußball? — Yes/no questions need the verb first (V-S-O) — you can't just add a question mark to a normal statement order.
  • Sprichst du Italienisch? (to a teacher) → Sprechen Sie Italienisch? — du is for friends and family; teachers and strangers get Sie. Using du with an adult you don't know well sounds impolite.
  • haben sie zeit? (lowercase sie) → Haben Sie Zeit? — Formal Sie is always capitalized, even mid-sentence — lowercase 'sie' means 'she/they', a completely different word.
  • zehndrei (for 13) → dreizehn — German numbers 13-19 put the digit first, then -zehn (ten): drei+zehn, not zehn+drei.
  • sechszehn (for 16) → sechzehn — sechs drops its s before -zehn — the correct spelling is sechzehn, not sechszehn.
  • Wie alt ist er? — Ich verstehe nicht. → Wie alt ist er? — Ich weiß nicht. — 'Ich verstehe nicht' means you didn't understand the question itself; if you understood it but don't know the answer, say 'Ich weiß nicht.'
  • zehnzig or zweizig (for 20) → zwanzig — 20 is an irregular word on its own, not built from zwei the way 13-19 are built from their digits plus -zehn.
  • Using 'Vielleicht' to mean 'no' → Vielleicht means 'maybe' — a genuine middle option between Ja and Nein. — Vielleicht is not a soft no; it is a real third answer, and collapsing it into 'nein' changes your meaning.
  • Ich wohnst in Mirpurkhas. → Ich wohne in Mirpurkhas. — ich always takes -e, never -st — -st belongs only to du.
11

Personalpronomen (Nominativ) (Personal Pronouns (Nominative))

One small word decides everything — who's speaking, who's listening, and how polite you need to be. Master this grid tonight and half of tomorrow's sentences fall into place.

Die Regel (the pronoun grid this Lektion is built on)

1 · Pronomen ersetzen Nomen (pronouns replace nouns)

German Personalpronomen (personal pronouns) do exactly what English pronouns do — they stand in for a noun you've already mentioned, so you don't have to repeat it. Instead of saying a name twice, you say er, sie, or es (he/she/it).

2 · Drei Personen, zwei Zahlen (three persons, two numbers)

Every pronoun has a Person (who's talking) and a number (how many). Erste Person = the speaker (ich/wir); zweite Person = the one spoken to (du/ihr); dritte Person = the one spoken about (er/sie/es/sie). Learn the whole grid, not just the individual words.

3 · sie hat zwei Bedeutungen — und Sie ist die dritte (sie has two meanings — and Sie is the third · exam tip)

Watch this trap on the test: lowercase sie means both she and they — identical spelling, identical sound. Capital Sie is a completely different word: the formal you, always written with a capital letter no matter where it sits in the sentence. If you spot a capital S in the middle of a sentence, it's the polite you — not a mistake.

4 · Die Verbendung folgt dem Pronomen (the verb ending follows the pronoun)

The pronoun decides the verb's ending. With ich, wohnen becomes wohne (I live); with wir, it stays wohnen (we live) — identical to the dictionary form. Memorise these two now; the rest of the conjugation pattern you'll meet later builds directly on them.

Fachbegriffe (grammar terms this Lektion needs)

  • 🔤Pronomenpronoun pro-NOH-men · — stands in for a noun so you don't repeat it: Ali ist müde. Er schläft. instead of Ali ist müde. Ali schläft. neutral
  • 🙋erste Personfirst person EHR-steh pehr-ZOHN · — the one speaking: ich and wir. neutral
  • 👉zweite Personsecond person TSVAI-teh pehr-ZOHN · — the one spoken to: du (informal singular) and ihr (informal plural). neutral
  • 👤dritte Personthird person DRIT-teh pehr-ZOHN · — the one spoken about: er, sie, es, sie. neutral
  • 1️⃣Singularsingular ZING-goo-lar · — one person: ich, du, er/sie/es. neutral
  • 👥Pluralplural PLOO-rahl · — more than one: wir, ihr, sie. neutral
Personalpronomen · Nominativ (personal pronouns · subject case — learn the whole grid)
Singular (singular)Plural (plural)
1. Person (first person · speaker)ichwir
2. Person, informell (second person, informal · spoken to)duihr
3. Person (third person · spoken about)er / sie / essie
Höflichkeitsform (formal you · singular or plural)Sie

Pronomen (the pronouns themselves)

  • 🙋ichI ISH · — always lowercase mid-sentence, unlike English "I" (a soft, breathy ch, not a sharp "sh"). neutral
  • 👥wirwe veer · — the plural of ich: the group that includes the speaker. neutral
  • 👉duyou (informal, singular) doo · — use with friends, family, children, and people your own age. informell
  • 👉👉ihryou (informal, plural — "you all") eer · — the plural of du: a group of people you know informally. informell
  • 👨erhe / it air · — used for masculine nouns too, not just male people: der Tisch becomes er. neutral
  • 👩sie (she)she / it zee · — used for feminine nouns too: die Tür becomes sie. neutral
  • 🔘esit ess · — used for neuter (das) nouns: das Kind becomes es, even for a person. neutral
  • 👨‍👩‍👧sie (they)they zee · — spelled and sounds exactly like "she" — only the verb form or context tells them apart. neutral
  • 🤝Sieyou (formal, singular & plural) ZEE, capital S · — always capitalised, even mid-sentence: the capital letter is what marks it as the polite "you". formell

Verb & Präposition (verb & preposition)

  • 🏠wohnento live (reside) VOH-nen · — a regular verb: its wir-form looks identical to the infinitive — wir wohnen. neutral
  • 📍inin in · — tells you where someone lives, here followed directly by a place name. neutral

Beispiele (the two model sentences this Lektion drills)

  • 💬Ich wohne in Mirpur-khas.I live in Mirpur-khas. ish VOH-neh in MEER-poor-khahs · — the model sentence for ich + wohnen: swap in any city name to talk about yourself. neutral
  • 💬Wir wohnen in Mirpur.We live in Mirpur. veer VOH-nen in MEER-poor · — wir + wohnen: the verb ends in -en, exactly matching the infinitive form. neutral

Nomen aus dieser Lektion (nouns from this lesson — look at the article, not just the word)

  • 🔤das Pronomen / die Pronomenpronoun — plural looks the same as the singular.
  • 🧍die Person / die Personenperson
  • 1️⃣der Singular / die Singularesingular — the plural form is Singulare.
  • 👥der Plural / die Pluraleplural — the plural form is Plurale.

Dialog 1 — Ich wohne, wir wohnen (dialogue · introducing where you live)

👋 Hina
Hallo!Hi!
🙋‍♀️ Sana
Hallo, Hina!Hi, Hina!
👋 Hina
Ich wohne in Mirpur-khas.I live in Mirpur-khas.
🙋‍♀️ Sana
Wir wohnen in Mirpur.We live in Mirpur.
👋 Hina
Tschüss!Bye!
🙋‍♀️ Sana
Tschüss!Bye!

Ich wohne (-e ending) versus wir wohnen (-en ending, identical to the infinitive) — the two nominative persons this Lektion drills hardest.

Dialog 2 — Er, sie oder es? (dialogue · he, she, or it — matching pronouns to a noun's gender)

🧑‍🏫 Lehrer (teacher)
Der Tisch — er, sie oder es?The table — he, she, or it?
🙋‍♀️ Schülerin (student)
Er!He (it)!
🧑‍🏫 Lehrer (teacher)
Ja! Der Tisch — er.Yes! The table — er.
🧑‍🏫 Lehrer (teacher)
Das Kind — er, sie oder es?The child — he, she, or it?
🙋‍♀️ Schülerin (student)
Es!It!
🧑‍🏫 Lehrer (teacher)
Ja! Das Kind — es.Yes! The child — es.

This is exactly how German assigns er/sie/es — by the noun's grammatical article (der/die/das), not by whether it's a person, animal, or object.

Dialog 3 — Du oder ihr? (dialogue · one friend or a group — du versus ihr)

Ayesha sees her friend Sana on the street.
🙋‍♀️ Ayesha
Hallo, Sana!Hi, Sana!
👩 Sana
Hallo, Ayesha! Wie geht's?Hi, Ayesha! How are you?
Two more friends arrive and join them.
🙋‍♀️ Ayesha
Hallo, ihr!Hi, you two!
👥 Freunde (friends)
Hallo, Ayesha!Hi, Ayesha!

Ayesha greets one friend by name (du is implied), then switches to ihr the instant she's addressing more than one person informally.

Dialog 4 — Sie oder du? (dialogue · formal or informal — greeting a teacher versus a friend)

A student greets her teacher formally, then greets her friend informally.
🙋‍♀️ Schülerin (student)
Guten Tag! Ich wohne in Mirpur.Good day! I live in Mirpur.
🧑‍🏫 Lehrerin (teacher)
Wohnen Sie in Mirpur-khas?Do you (formal) live in Mirpur-khas?
🙋‍♀️ Schülerin (student)
Nein. Und Sie?No. And you?
🧑‍🏫 Lehrerin (teacher)
Ich wohne in Mirpur-khas.I live in Mirpur-khas.

Sie takes the same -en verb ending as wir (wohnen) — but because it's the formal "you", it's always capitalized, even in the middle of a question.

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · Aussage: Subjekt + Verb (-e) + Rest — die ich-Form (statement: subject + verb + the rest — the ich form)
IchSubjekt · subjectwohneVerb · verb, position 2, -ein Mirpur-khas.Ort · place

With ich the verb takes -e: wohnen → ich wohne. The verb still sits in position 2, exactly like every German statement — now with a real subject pronoun filling slot one.

2 · Aussage: Subjekt + Verb (-en) + Rest — die wir-Form (statement: subject + verb + the rest — the wir form)
WirSubjekt · subjectwohnenVerb · verb, position 2, -enin Mirpur.Ort · place

With wir the verb keeps the full infinitive ending -en: wohnen → wir wohnen. Same slot, same position — only the ending on the verb changes.

3 · Das Pronomen ersetzt das ganze Subjekt (the pronoun replaces the whole subject)
Der TischSubjekt · subject, masculineistVerb · verbalt.Adjektiv · adjective
ErSubjekt · subject; replaces "der Tisch"istVerb · verbalt.Adjektiv · adjective

The whole subject slot gets swapped, not just the noun: der Tisch → er, because Tisch is a der-word. Gender comes from the article, never from real life — das Kind (a person!) still becomes es.

4 · Ja/Nein-Frage mit Sie: Verb + Sie + Rest? (yes/no question with formal Sie: verb + Sie + the rest?)
WohnenVerb · verb, position 1Sieformelles Sie · formal youin Mirpur-khas?Ort · place

A yes/no question puts the verb first, exactly as in earlier Lektionen — only now the subject slot holds the formal Sie. Answered with Nein. Und Sie? — the short question that hands the topic straight back.

5 · Sie, sie (they) und wir haben dieselbe -en-Endung (Sie, sie meaning “they,” and wir share the -en ending)
Sieformell · formal SiewohnenVerb · verb, -en wie wirin Mirpur-khas.Ort · place

Sie (formal you), lowercase sie (they) and wir all conjugate the same way, with -en. Mid-sentence, the capital letter distinguishes formal Sie from sie; at the start of a sentence, context must tell you which meaning is intended.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • ich — leise gesagt (ich — said softly): Say it softly, almost like a breath, not a sharp "ish" — the quietest word for the biggest subject: yourself.
  • wir — wie "we're" (wir — like “we're”): wir sounds like the start of "we're" — and that's exactly what it means: "we are" the group.
  • du vs. Sie (informal vs. formal “you”): du is for people you'd hug; Sie is for people you'd shake hands with. If you're unsure with an elder or a stranger, go with capital Sie.
  • er / sie / es — folge dem Artikel (follow the article): Never ask "is it male or female in real life?" — ask "is the noun der, die, or das?" der→er, die→sie, das→es. The pronoun copies the article's gender, not the object's.
  • sie vs. Sie — gleicher Klang, andere Schreibung (same sound, different spelling): Same sound, different size: lowercase sie hides quietly inside a sentence (she/they); capital Sie always stands tall (formal you) — mid-sentence, the capital letter is your clue.
  • ihr — du plus deine Crew (ihr — du plus your crew): ihr is just du with friends added — think "you plus your crew".
  • wohnen — denk an Wohnzimmer (think of Wohnzimmer): wohnen looks like "wohn-" (home) + "-en" — picture your Wohnzimmer (living room) every time you conjugate it.
  • ich wohne / wir wohnen (I live / we live): One person, one -e; a group, -en. Fewer letters for fewer people: ich wohn-E, wir wohn-EN.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • Ich wohnt in Mirpur-khas. → Ich wohne in Mirpur-khas. — ich pairs with the -e ending (wohne), not -t — wohnt belongs to a different subject entirely.
  • wir wohne in Mirpur. → Wir wohnen in Mirpur. — wir needs the -en ending, identical to the infinitive wohnen, and it is capitalised as Wir at the start of the sentence.
  • der Tisch → sie → der Tisch → er — masculine nouns (der) are replaced by er, not sie — go by the article, not by imagining a gender.
  • das Kind → sie → das Kind → es — das Kind is grammatically neuter, so it becomes es, even though the actual child is a girl or boy.
  • wohnen sie in Mirpur-khas? (addressing a teacher, lowercase s) → Wohnen Sie in Mirpur-khas? — the formal "you" is always capitalized — Sie — even mid-sentence; lowercase sie would mean "they" or "she" instead.
  • Talking to one friend: 'Hallo, ihr!' → Hallo, [Name]! / addressing them as du — ihr is only for two or more people you're addressing informally; for a single friend, du (or their name) is correct.
  • Talking to a group of friends: 'Hallo, du!' → Hallo, ihr! — when more than one person is being addressed informally, switch to ihr, the plural of du.
  • Calling wir a 'zweite Person' pronoun → wir is erste Person (plural) — students often assume more people means a different "person" category, but wir is still first person, because it's the speaker (plus others) talking, not being talked to.
12

Haben und Sein — Konjugation (Conjugating 'to have' and 'to be')

Haben and sein are the two verbs almost every German sentence leans on — and both are irregular, so there's no shortcut except memorizing the full tables. Watch one quiet trap: your own notes say 'du habst', but the correct standard form is 'du hast'.

Die Regel (the two irregular verbs this Lektion turns on)

Zwei Hilfsverben (two auxiliary verbs)

Every A1 course leans on two verbs above all others: haben (to have) and sein (to be). Neither follows the normal -e/-st/-t/-en pattern regular verbs use — both are irregular, so there is no shortcut except memorizing the full table cold.

🗒️

Haben — Konjugation (Prüfungstipp) (conjugating haben — exam tip)

The pattern for haben is habe / hast / hat / haben / habt / haben. Watch er/sie/es hat — the 'b' drops, unlike ihr habt, which keeps it. Exam tip: the correct standard form for 'du' is du hast — you may have written 'habst' in your notebook, but that is not correct German, so write hast on your test.

🗒️

Sein — komplett unregelmäßig (sein — completely irregular)

sein is even more irregular than haben — bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind barely resemble the infinitive at all. There's no pattern to lean on here; treat it like a short chant to memorize by sound.

🗒️

Fragen: Verb zuerst (questions: verb first)

In a yes/no question, the verb jumps to the front of the sentence: Hast du...?, Habt ihr...?, Sind Sie...? — it's the exact same haben/sein form you already know, just moved to position one.

🗒️

Konjugation — haben (conjugation — to have)

  • 🙋ich habeI have ihh HAH-be · · Drop the -en of the infinitive haben, add -e — this is the 'ich' pattern for almost every verb.
  • 👉du hastyou have (informal) doo hust · · The correct standard form — some notes write 'habst', but German only ever says hast.
  • 🙂er/sie/es hathe/she/it has air/zee/es hut · · The 'b' disappears here — hat, not habt, which belongs to ihr instead.
  • 👥wir habenwe have veer HAH-ben · · Matches the plain infinitive haben exactly — easy to remember as 'the dictionary form'.
  • 👉👉ihr habtyou all have (informal plural) eer hahpt · · Pronounced like 'hahpt' — the written 'b' is pronounced as a 'p' before 't'.
  • 🤝sie/Sie habenthey have / you have (formal) zee HAH-ben · · One word covers both 'they have' and the polite 'you have' — only capitalization tells them apart in writing.

Konjugation — sein (conjugation — to be)

  • 🙋ich binI am ihh bin · · Totally irregular — it doesn't resemble the infinitive sein at all, so just memorize it.
  • 👉du bistyou are (informal) doo bist · · Easy to confuse with 'hast' — bist is being (sein), hast is having (haben).
  • 🙂er/sie/es isthe/she/it is air/zee/es ist · · The single most common form of sein — you'll use it constantly to describe people and things.
  • 👥wir sindwe are veer zint · · wir and sie take sind; formal Sie also takes sind for one person or a group, while ihr takes seid.
  • 👉👉ihr seidyou all are (informal plural) eer zyte · · Sounds identical to 'seit' (since) — same pronunciation, completely different word and spelling.
  • 🤝sie/Sie sindthey are / you are (formal) zee zint · · Same word for 'they are' and polite 'you are' — just like haben, capitalization is the only clue.
haben & sein (to have & to be) · Konjugation nebeneinander (conjugation side by side)
Pronomen (pronouns)haben (to have)sein (to be)
ich (I)habebin
du (you)hastbist
er / sie / es (he/she/it)hatist
wir (we)habensind
ihr (you all)habtseid
sie / Sie (they/you formal)habensind

Vokabel (vocabulary)

  • 😊glücklichhappy GLIK-lish · · An adjective describing a state — pairs naturally with sein.
  • 💍verheiratetmarried fair-HY-rah-tet · · Break it into fer-HEIRAT-et; 'Heirat' hidden inside means marriage.
  • 👩‍🏫die Lehrerin / die Lehrerinnenteacher (female) LAY-reh-rin · · The -in ending marks the feminine form; a male teacher is 'Lehrer' (Lektion 19).
  • 🏘️der Nachbar / die Nachbarnneighbor / neighbors NAHKH-bar / NAHKH-barn · /ˈnaxbaːɐ̯/, · 'Meine Nachbarn' (plural) takes sind, not ist — plural subject, plural verb.
  • 🤗nettnice, kind net · · A short, extremely common adjective in everyday German.
  • 💯sehrvery zair · · Sits directly before the adjective it strengthens: sehr nett.
  • 🏠zu Hauseat home tsoo HOW-zeh · · A fixed phrase — don't translate word-for-word; it simply means 'at home'.

Beispiel (examples)

  • 🚗Ich habe ein Auto.I have a car. ihh HAH-be ine OW-toh · · Auto is neuter, so it takes ein, never einen or eine.
  • 🏠Ich habe ein Haus.I have a house. ihh HAH-be ine house · · Haus is also neuter — the same ein pattern as Auto.
  • 🚗Wir haben ein Auto.We have a car. veer HAH-ben ine OW-toh · · Same sentence pattern as 'Ich habe ein Auto' — just swap the subject and haben form.
  • ⏰Er hat keine Zeit.He has no time. air hut KY-neh tsyte · · keine (not kein) because Zeit is feminine — this is the negative form of eine.
  • 👧Maria hat eine Tochter.Maria has a daughter. mah-REE-ah hut EYE-neh TOKH-ter · · Tochter is feminine, so eine — and hat because Maria is 'she' (er/sie/es).
  • 🐕Meine Eltern haben einen Hund.My parents have a dog. MY-neh EL-tern HAH-ben EYE-nen hoont · · Eltern is plural, so it takes haben, not hat — and Hund is masculine, so einen (Lektion 27).
  • 🎂Ich bin 16 Jahre alt.I am 16 years old. ihh bin ZEKH-tsayn YAH-reh ult · · Age uses sein (bin), not haben — a very common beginner slip if your first language says 'I have 16 years'.
  • 😊Wir sind glücklich.We are happy. veer zint GLIK-lish · · Subject wir triggers sind — a simple, complete statement with sein.
  • 💍Er ist verheiratet.He is married. air ist fair-HY-rah-tet · · er takes ist, the same pattern as sie and es.
  • 👩‍🏫Sabine ist Lehrerin.Sabine is a teacher. zah-BEE-neh ist LAY-reh-rin · · No article before a profession after sein — not 'ist eine Lehrerin'.
  • 🏘️Meine Nachbarn sind sehr nett.My neighbors are very nice. MY-neh NAHKH-barn zint zair net · · Plural subject Nachbarn needs sind, and sehr sits right before nett.

Frage (questions)

  • ❓Hast du eine Freundin?Do you have a girlfriend? hast doo EYE-neh FROYN-din · · Yes/no questions put the verb first: Hast du...? not Du hast...?
  • 💍Sind Sie verheiratet?Are you married? (formal) zint zee fair-HY-rah-tet · · verheiratet pairs with sein, not haben — 'being' married, not 'having' married.
  • 👶Habt ihr Kinder?Do you all have children? hahpt eer KIN-der · · Kinder appears with no article here — plural nouns often drop it in general questions like this.
  • ⏱️Frau Schmidt, haben Sie einen Moment?Mrs. Schmidt, do you have a moment? frow shmit, HAH-ben zee EYE-nen moh-MENT · · Moment is masculine, so einen — and the polite Sie always pairs with haben, never habt.
  • 😊Seid ihr glücklich?Are you (all) happy? zite eer GLIK-lish · · Yes/no question: the verb seid jumps to the front, before ihr.
  • 🏠Frau Schmidt, sind Sie zu Hause?Mrs. Schmidt, are you at home? frow shmit, zint zee tsoo HOW-zeh · · A polite question using capital Sie — right for addressing an adult by title and surname.

Dialoge (six short conversations built from this Lektion's own example sentences)

1 · Zwei Freunde (two friends chatting)
👧 Sara
Hallo Ali! Hast du ein Auto?Hi Ali! Do you have a car?
🧑 Ali
Nein, ich habe kein Auto. Ich habe ein Haus.No, I don't have a car. I have a house.
👧 Sara
Hast du eine Freundin?Do you have a girlfriend?
🧑 Ali
Ja, ich habe eine Freundin. Wir haben einen Hund.Yes, I have a girlfriend. We have a dog.
🧑 Ali
Ich bin 16 Jahre alt. Und du?I am 16 years old. And you?
👧 Sara
Ich bin auch 16 Jahre alt.I am also 16 years old.

💡Notice how haben (habe/hast/haben) handles all the 'having' — car, house, girlfriend, dog — while sein (bin) is the only verb used for age, exactly as in the source examples.

2 · Im Büro (at the office)
👔 Chef
Frau Schmidt, haben Sie einen Moment?Mrs. Schmidt, do you have a moment?
👩‍💼 Frau Schmidt
Ja, ich habe Zeit.Yes, I have time.
👔 Chef
Gut. Sind Sie verheiratet?Good. Are you married?
👩‍💼 Frau Schmidt
Nein. Ich habe eine Tochter.No. I have a daughter.
👔 Chef
Haben Sie einen Hund?Do you have a dog?
👩‍💼 Frau Schmidt
Nein.No.

💡A fully formal exchange: every question uses the Sie form of haben and sein (haben Sie / Sind Sie) — the same form whether 'Sie' means one polite person or a polite group.

3 · Meine Eltern (my parents)
🧑 Ali
Meine Eltern haben einen Hund.My parents have a dog.
👧 Sara
Habt ihr auch ein Auto?Do you all also have a car?
🧑 Ali
Ja, wir haben ein Auto und ein Haus.Yes, we have a car and a house.
👧 Sara
Hat Maria eine Tochter?Does Maria have a daughter?
🧑 Ali
Ja, Maria hat eine Tochter.Yes, Maria has a daughter.

💡This one conversation cycles through nearly every haben form — haben (Eltern/wir), habt (ihr), and hat (Maria) — all built from the lesson's own example sentences.

4 · Sind Sie zu Hause? (a polite phone call)
📞 Anna
Guten Tag, Frau Schmidt. Sind Sie zu Hause?Good day, Mrs. Schmidt. Are you at home?
👩‍💼 Frau Schmidt
Ja, ich bin zu Hause.Yes, I am at home.
📞 Anna
Gut! Sind Sie glücklich?Good! Are you happy?
👩‍💼 Frau Schmidt
Ja, ich bin sehr glücklich.Yes, I am very happy.

💡Notice the switch: Anna asks using the formal Sie + sind, but Frau Schmidt answers about herself using ich + bin — the form always follows the subject, not who is speaking.

5 · Seid ihr glücklich? (talking to a group of friends)
🙋 Tom
Hallo! Seid ihr glücklich?Hi! Are you (all) happy?
🙆‍♀️ Lena
Ja, wir sind sehr glücklich.Yes, we are very happy.
🙋 Tom
Ich spiele Fußball. Und ihr?I play football. And you (all)?
🙆‍♀️ Lena
Wir sind zu Hause.We are at home.

💡This dialogue puts the informal group form ihr/seid next to wir/sind, and drops in a regular verb (spiele, Lektion 13) beside the irregular sein forms.

6 · Wer ist Sabine? (asking about someone)
🗣️ Petra
Ist Sabine Lehrerin?Is Sabine a teacher?
🧑‍🎓 Yusuf
Ja, Sabine ist Lehrerin. Sie ist auch verheiratet.Yes, Sabine is a teacher. She is also married.
🗣️ Petra
Ist sie nett?Is she nice?
🧑‍🎓 Yusuf
Ja, sie ist sehr nett.Yes, she is very nice.

💡Every subject here — Sabine, sie — is singular, so ist appears every time; also notice there is no article before the profession Lehrerin.

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · Aussage: Subjekt + haben + Objekt (Akkusativ) (statement: subject + to have + object, accusative)
IchSubjekt · subjecthabeVerb · position 2ein Auto.Objekt · object, Akkusativ · accusative

When haben expresses possession, its direct object is in the accusative: Ich habe ein Auto / ein Haus. Auto and Haus are both neuter, so the object keeps the plain ein — masculine objects change to einen (Lektion 27), as in einen Hund and einen Moment.

2 · Aussage: Subjekt + sein + Rest — kein Objekt (statement: subject + to be + the rest — no object)
WirSubjekt · subjectsindVerb · position 2glücklich.Adjektiv · adjective/predicate, nicht Akkusativ · not accusative

sein never takes an accusative object — it links the subject to a predicate instead: an adjective (glücklich, verheiratet, nett), a place (zu Hause) or a profession (Lehrerin). Compare Ich habe ein Auto (object) with Ich bin glücklich (predicate) — the two verbs behave completely differently after them.

3 · Alter: sein, nicht haben (age: to be, not to have)
IchSubjekt · subjectbinVerb · position 216 Jahre alt.Alter · age, kein Besitz · not possession

German states age with sein, never haben: Ich bin 16 Jahre alt. Saying Ich habe 16 Jahre alt is a classic beginner slip if your first language 'has' an age instead of 'being' one (see Korrekturen below).

4 · Ja/Nein-Frage: Verb zuerst (yes/no question: verb first)
HastVerb · position 1duSubjekt · subjecteine Freundin?Akkusativ · accusative

Yes/no questions move the conjugated verb to the very front, before the subject: Hast du...?, Habt ihr Kinder?, Sind Sie verheiratet? — the exact same haben/sein form you already memorised, only the position changes.

5 · ihr vs. Sie — seid vs. sind (Prüfungstipp) (informal vs. formal you — exam tip)
Seidinformell · informal · ihrihrSubjekt · subjectglücklich?Rest · the rest
Sindformell · formal · SieSieSubjekt · subjectzu Hause?Rest · the rest

When addressing a group, both ihr and Sie can translate as 'you', but they never share a verb form; Sie can also address one person formally. Informal ihr always pairs with seid (Seid ihr glücklich?), while formal Sie always pairs with sind (Sind Sie zu Hause?).

6 · Beruf nach sein: kein Artikel (profession after to be: no article)
SabineSubjekt · subjectistVerb · position 2Lehrerin.Beruf · profession, kein Artikel · no article

After sein, an unmodified profession drops its article: Sabine ist Lehrerin, not "ist eine Lehrerin" (see Korrekturen). The -in ending marks the feminine form of a profession, as in Lektion 19.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • Merkhilfen — haben (memory hooks): du hast — You HAVE STuff — hast, no 'b'. The 'b' returns in the forms haben and habt. er/sie/es hat — one person, one short word: hat; carrying the 'b' alone got too heavy, so he dropped it. ihr habt — pronounced "hahpt": picture the whole group carrying the written 'b' together. sie/Sie haben — whether it's 'they' or polite 'You', the full form is haben.
  • Merkhilfen — sein (memory hooks): ich bin — bin has no relatives in the sein family; anchor it alone: "I bin here, just me." du bist — bist rhymes with "wrist": you ARE a person with a wrist. wir/sie/Sie sind — these three subjects land on sind, like a bond tying them together; informal ihr is the exception and takes seid. ihr seid — seid looks like "said": imagine you SAID something to the whole group.
  • Ich bin 16 Jahre alt (I am 16 years old): age is a state of being, not a possession, so German uses sein (bin), never haben — you don't 'have' 16, you 'are' 16.
  • Er hat keine Zeit (He has no time): keine, not kein, because Zeit is feminine (the ein/kein pattern from Lektion 20–21). Treat the source's “soft ending” image only as a memory hook, not as a rule for predicting noun gender.
  • haben's object is accusative, sein's is not. Masculine objects of haben change ein → einen: einen Hund, einen Moment (Lektion 27). Feminine and neuter objects stay ein/eine: ein Auto, eine Tochter. sein instead links to a bare predicate with no case change at all.
  • sehr nett (very nice): say it fast — "zair net" — picture a very (sehr) kind net (nett) catching you when you fall. sehr always sits directly before the adjective it strengthens.
  • zu Hause (at home) — a false friend: Hause looks like "house", but zu Hause means AT home, as if you've already arrived — not still heading there. Don't translate it word-for-word.
  • verheiratet (married): hidden inside is Heirat (marriage) — ver- + Heirat + -et wraps the whole institution into one word; pairs with sein, never haben.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • du habst → du hast — Standard German always uses hast for du; habst is not a correct form, even if it appears written that way somewhere in your notes.
  • er habt → er hat — habt belongs only to ihr. For er/sie/es, the 'b' drops and it becomes hat.
  • Ich bin ein Auto. → Ich habe ein Auto. — Possession needs haben. sein only means 'to be', never 'to have'; saying "Ich bin ein Auto" means "I am a car".
  • Ich habe 16 Jahre alt. → Ich bin 16 Jahre alt. — German states age with sein, not haben, even though it can feel like you should 'have' an age.
  • Wir sind ein Auto. → Wir haben ein Auto. — Same haben/sein mix-up with wir — "Wir sind ein Auto" would mean "We are a car".
  • Ihr seid Kinder? → Habt ihr Kinder? — 'To have children' needs haben. "Ihr seid Kinder?" actually asks "Are you all children?" — a completely different question.
  • Sie habt einen Moment? → Haben Sie einen Moment? — habt is only for ihr. The polite Sie always takes haben, matching wir and sie.
  • Du bin verheiratet? → Bist du verheiratet? / Sind Sie verheiratet? — bin is only for ich. du needs bist (informal) and Sie needs sind (formal).
  • Ich sind glücklich. → Ich bin glücklich. — ich always pairs with bin, never sind — sind belongs only to wir/sie/Sie.
  • Wir bin glücklich. → Wir sind glücklich. — wir takes sind, not bin — bin is reserved for ich alone.
  • Seid Sie zu Hause? → Sind Sie zu Hause? — Formal Sie always takes sind, even though it looks like 'you' the way ihr does — seid is only for informal ihr.
  • Sind ihr glücklich? → Seid ihr glücklich? — ihr must pair with seid, not sind — this is the single most common mix-up between the two plural 'you' forms.
  • Meine Nachbarn ist sehr nett. → Meine Nachbarn sind sehr nett. — Nachbarn is plural, so it needs the plural verb sind, not the singular ist.
  • Sabine ist eine Lehrerin. → Sabine ist Lehrerin. — German drops the article before an unmodified profession after sein — say ist Lehrerin, not ist eine Lehrerin.
  • Er sind verheiratet. → Er ist verheiratet. — er/sie/es always takes ist, never sind.
  • Glücklich ich bin. → Ich bin glücklich. — German statements put the subject first and the verb in second position — not the adjective before the subject.
13

Einführung in Verben & „sein“ (Introduction to Verbs & "to be")

Every German sentence pivots on its verb — and sein, the most important verb of all, changes shape for every single person. Today you nail down all six forms and the ihr/Sie trap examiners love to test.

Die Regel (the rule this Lektion turns on)

Was ist ein Verb? (what is a verb?)

Every German sentence pivots on one word: the Verb — the action or state word. Change the verb, and the structure of the whole sentence shifts around it. Today's verb is the most important one in the language: sein — to be.

„sein“ verändert sich mit jeder Person (sein changes with every person)

German has no single word for 'is/am/are' — it has six, each tied to who is speaking or being spoken about: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind. Watch the pattern in the notes: Wir sind glücklich, Er ist verheiratet, Meine Nachbarn sind sehr nett — the verb form always matches the subject standing next to it.

Informelles ihr oder formelles Sie? (ihr vs. Sie — the exam trap)

Both ihr and Sie can be translated as 'you' when speaking to more than one person — but they take completely different verb forms. Ihr is informal, for people you know well, and pairs with seid: Seid ihr glücklich? Sie is the polite, capitalized form — used for one person or many — and always pairs with sind: Sind Sie zu Hause? Prüfungstipp: whenever you see a capital Sie, the verb beside it is always sind, never seid — this exact contrast is a favourite test question.

Regelmäßige Verben funktionieren anders: spielen (regular verbs behave differently: spielen)

Not every verb is as irregular as sein. Most German verbs are 'regular' and follow a predictable pattern: take the infinitive (dictionary form, ending in -en), drop the -en, and for ich add -e. So spielen — to play — becomes ich spiele: Ich spiele Fußball. Compare that to the irregular ich bin: regular verbs can be built by rule, but sein must simply be memorized.

Vokabel (vocabulary)

  • 🔤das Verb / die Verbenverb fairp · · the action/state word of a sentence — sein and spielen are both examples.
  • ▶️spielento play SHPEE-len · · a regular verb — the ich-form just drops -en and adds -e: spiele.
  • ⚽der Fußball / die Fußbällefootball / soccer FOOSS-bal · · no article needed — “Fußball spielen” is a fixed activity phrase.

Wortschatz aus den Regeln (vocabulary from the rules)

  • 😊glücklichhappy · from the notes: Wir sind glücklich, Seid ihr glücklich?
  • 💍verheiratetmarried · Er ist verheiratet.
  • 🤗nettnice · Meine Nachbarn sind sehr nett. (sehr = very)
  • 🏠zu Hauseat home · Sind Sie zu Hause?

Beispiel (example)

  • 💬Ich spiele Fußball.I play football. ish SHPEE-leh FOOSS-bal · · a regular-verb example — contrast spiele (-e ending) with the irregular bin.

Frage (question)

  • ❓Was ist ein Verb?What is a verb? vass ist eyen fairp · · was + ist + ein + noun is the pattern for “what is a ___?”.
sein (to be) · Konjugation (conjugation)
Pronomen (pronoun)sein (to be)Bedeutung (meaning)
ich (I)binam
du (you)bistare
er / sie / es (he / she / it)istis
wir (we)sindare
ihr (you all)seidare
sie / Sie (they / you formal)sindare

Dialog: Was ist ein Verb? (dialogue: what is a verb? — a student asks about grammar)

🙋 Schüler (student)
Was ist ein Verb?What is a verb?
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin (teacher)
Spielen ist ein Verb. Sein ist auch ein Verb.'To play' is a verb. 'To be' is also a verb.
🙋 Schüler (student)
Ich bin glücklich. Ich spiele Fußball.I am happy. I play football.

The student's last line puts both of this lesson's verbs to work: the irregular sein (bin) and the regular spielen (spiele).

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · W-Frage (W-question): Was + ist + ein + Nomen (noun)?
WasW-Wort · question wordistVerb · position 2ein Verb?Prädikatsnomen · predicate noun

Was ist ein Verb? (What is a verb?) is the pattern for any "what is a ___?" question: was + ist + ein + noun. The W-word opens the sentence, and the verb still holds position 2. Ein Verb is a predicate noun here, not an accusative object, so it is grey rather than amber.

2 · sein + Prädikativ: Subjekt + bin/ist/sind + Adjektiv (sein + predicate: subject + bin/ist/sind + adjective)
IchSubjekt · subjectbinsein · to be, position 2glücklich.Prädikativ · predicate adjective

With sein the word after the verb is not an accusative object — it describes the subject, so it is grey (Rest), not amber. Ich bin glücklich. (from the dialogue) and Er ist verheiratet. (from the rule) both follow this pattern.

3 · sein always agrees with the subject
WirSubjekt · subjectsindsein · to be, position 2glücklich.Prädikativ · predicate adjectiveMeine NachbarnSubjekt · plural subjectsindsein · to besehr nett.Prädikativ · predicate adjective

The six person forms — ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind — always match the subject. A plural subject such as meine Nachbarn needs sind, exactly like wir.

4 · ihr vs. Sie — same meaning, different verb
SeidVerb · position 1ihrinformell · informalglücklich?Prädikativ · predicate adjectiveSindVerb · position 1Sieformell · formalzu Hause?Ort · place

Both questions mean roughly "are you...?", but ihr (people you know well) always takes seid, while capitalized Sie (the polite form, singular or plural) always takes sind — never seid. Examiners love to swap these two.

5 · Regelmäßiges Verb: Subjekt + Verb(-e) + Objekt (regular verb: subject + verb ending in -e + object)
IchSubjekt · subjectspieleregelmäßig · regular, -e endingFußball.feste Wendung · fixed phrase, no article

Unlike irregular sein, most verbs are regular: take the infinitive (spielen), drop -en, add -e for ich. In the activity phrase Fußball spielen, Fußball is an accusative object used without an article.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • Was ist = “what is”: Was ist closely matches English "what is" in meaning and loosely echoes it in sound — a friendly memory hook for this question opener.
  • Fußball spielen has no article: for the activity, say Ich spiele Fußball, not Ich spiele einen Fußball — like English "I play football," it needs no article here.
  • The full present tense of spielen: ich spiele, du spielst, er/sie/es spielt, wir spielen, ihr spielt, sie/Sie spielen — this shows the core regular pattern: -e / -st / -t / -en / -t / -en.
  • sein has two jobs — a German homonym: the verb sein (to be, today's lesson) is spelled exactly like the possessive sein (his/its, Lektion 24). A verb sits in position 2; a possessive sits right before a noun — context tells them apart.
  • sind vs. seid — don't let the spelling fool you: sind is pronounced roughly “zint” /zɪnt/; seid is roughly “zyte” /zaɪt/. They differ clearly in both vowel and final consonant.
  • das Verb is neuter: das Verb, plural die Verben — worth memorising alongside the meaning, since German grammar terms have genders too (also das Nomen, das Adjektiv).

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • Ich spielen Fußball. → Ich spiele Fußball. — spielen is the infinitive (dictionary form); the ich-form drops -en and adds -e: spiele.
14

Regelmäßige und unregelmäßige Verben (Regular and Irregular Verbs)

Every German verb is a stem plus an ending — but a handful of very common verbs sneak in a vowel change just for du and er/sie/es. Tomorrow's test will try to catch you exactly there, so this lesson drills the six persons, the six regular endings, and the sprechen → du sprichst pattern until it's automatic.

Die Regel (how a German verb builds itself, person by person)

1 · Grundstruktur: Stamm + Endung (basic structure: stem + ending)

German verbs in the present tense are built from two parts that never get mixed up: the Verbstamm (the part before -en in the infinitive, e.g. mach- from machen) and the Endung (the ending that changes depending on who is doing the action). The stem usually stays fixed; only the ending moves.

2 · Regelmäßige Verben — die sechs Endungen (regular verbs — the six endings)

Regular verbs (regelmäßige Verben) like machen, wohnen, spielen, studieren, heißen and arbeiten add a fixed set of endings to the stem and never touch the stem vowel: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en. So machen → ich mache, du machst, er macht, wir machen, ihr macht, sie machen. These are the underlying endings; du heißt and du arbeitest / ihr arbeitet make the spelling or pronunciation adjustments explained below.

3 · Unregelmäßige Verben — Stammveränderung (irregular verbs — stem change)

Irregular verbs (unregelmäßige Verben) like sprechen, essen, sehen, nehmen, treffen, fahren and schlafen use the exact same endings — but only in du and er/sie/es, the stem vowel itself changes. sprechen → du sprichst, er spricht (e becomes i). This is the single most common trap in beginner tests: the endings are regular, the vowel is not.

4 · Prüfungstipp: ich, wir, ihr, sie/Sie bleiben treu (exam tip: ich, wir, ihr, sie/Sie keep the stem vowel)

With the stem-changing verbs in this lesson, the ich, wir, ihr, and sie/Sie forms never change their stem vowel — only du and er/sie/es do. So if a test asks you to conjugate essen for wir, the safe, boring answer wir essen is exactly right; the danger only lives in the du/er row.

Regelmäßiges Verb (regular verbs — six fixed endings, the vowel never moves)

  • 🏷️heißento be called / to be named HY-sən · — Because the stem ends in -ß, the du-form uses -t instead of -st: heiß+t = du heißt, not heißst.
  • 🏠wohnento live (reside) VOH-nən · — Ich wohne in Lahore — pairs naturally with a city or address.
  • 🛠️machento do / to make MAH-khən · — The model verb for the six regular endings: mache, machst, macht, machen, macht, machen.
  • ⚽spielento play SHPEE-lən · — Works for games, sports and instruments: Fußball spielen, Klavier spielen.
  • 🎓studierento study (at university) shtoo-DEE-rən · — Means being enrolled in a subject — different from lernen, "to study for a test".
  • 💼arbeitento work AR-by-tən · — Stem ends in -t, so du and ihr get an extra e: du arbeitest, ihr arbeitet.

Unregelmäßiges Verb (irregular verbs — the vowel changes only in du and er/sie/es)

  • 🗣️sprechento speak SHPREH-khən · — The lesson's key example: e becomes i in du/er — du sprichst, er spricht.
  • 😴schlafento sleep SHLAH-fən · — Different pattern from sprechen: a→ä, not e→i — du schläfst, er schläft.
  • 🍽️essento eat ES-sən · — e→i, and du merges with er in spelling: both are isst.
  • 👀sehento see ZAY-ən · — Changes further to ie, not just i: du siehst, er sieht.
  • 🤲nehmento take NAY-mən · — e→i, plus the h drops and the m doubles: du nimmst, er nimmt.
  • 🤝treffento meet TREF-fən · — Same e→i pattern as sprechen: du triffst, er trifft.
  • 🚗fahrento drive / to go (by vehicle) FAH-rən · — a→ä like schlafen: du fährst, er fährt.

Beispiel (du-Form) (examples — the du-form of each irregular verb above)

  • 🗣️du sprichstyou speak (informal) doo SHPRIHKHST · — From sprechen — the textbook example of the e→i change. informell
  • 🍽️du isstyou eat doo IST · — From essen — spelled identically to er isst, so context tells you who. informell
  • 👀du siehstyou see doo ZEEST · — From sehen — e stretches all the way to ie. informell
  • 🤲du nimmstyou take doo NIMST · — From nehmen — watch the double m and the dropped h. informell
  • 🤝du triffstyou meet doo TRIFST · — From treffen — same e→i pattern as sprichst. informell
  • 🚗du fährstyou drive doo FAIRST · — From fahren — a→ä, an umlaut appears out of nowhere. informell
  • 😴du schläfstyou sleep doo SHLAYFST · — From schlafen — a→ä, same family as fährst. informell
machen vs. sprechen · Präsens (regular vs. irregular conjugation, present tense — same endings, different vowel)

du (you, informal)machstsprichst

Nomen aus dieser Lektion (nouns from this lesson — look at the article, not just the word)

  • 🌱der Verbstamm / die Verbstämmeverb stem — the part of the verb before -en; its vowel changes only in specified forms of the stem-changing verbs taught here.
  • 🔤die Endung / die Endungenending — the part that changes to match who is doing the action.
  • 📅der Tag / die Tageday — from "jeden Tag" (every day) in Dialog 2.
  • 🕒die Uhr / die Uhrenclock / o'clock — from "um drei Uhr" (at three o'clock) in Dialog 3.
  • 🚌der Bus / die Bussebus — from the Korrektur "Du nimmst den Bus" (you take the bus).
  • ☕der Kaffee / die Kaffeescoffee — from the quiz sentence "Er nimmt jeden Tag Kaffee" (he has coffee every day); the plural is used for servings or varieties.

Dialog 1 — Wie heißt du? (introductions with fully regular verbs)

🙋‍♀️ Sara
Hallo! Wie heißt du?Hello! What are you called?
🧑 Ali
Ich heiße Ali. Und du?I'm called Ali. And you?
🙋‍♀️ Sara
Ich heiße Sara. Wo wohnst du?I'm called Sara. Where do you live?
🧑 Ali
Ich wohne in Lahore. Und du?I live in Lahore. And you?
🙋‍♀️ Sara
Ich wohne auch in Lahore!I also live in Lahore!

heißen and wohnen are both fully regular here — -e for ich, -st for du — with no stem-vowel change anywhere in the paradigm.

Dialog 2 — Was machst du heute? (talking about daily activities)

👨 Ahmed
Was machst du heute?What are you doing today?
👩 Fatima
Ich spiele Fußball. Und du?I'm playing football. And you?
👨 Ahmed
Ich arbeite heute. Ich arbeite jeden Tag.I'm working today. I work every day.
👩 Fatima
Und danach? Schläfst du früh?And afterward? Do you sleep early?
👨 Ahmed
Nein, ich schlafe spät. Ich studiere auch.No, I sleep late. I also study.

arbeiten inserts an extra e before the -st and -t endings to break up a difficult consonant cluster (arbeitest, arbeitet), while schlafen changes a to ä only in the du- and er/sie/es-forms: du schläfst, er schläft — ich schlafe stays untouched.

Dialog 3 — Sprichst du Deutsch? (testing sprechen, treffen and sehen side by side)

👧 Sana
Sprichst du Deutsch?Do you speak German?
🧑 Bilal
Ja, ich spreche ein bisschen Deutsch.Yes, I speak a little German.
👧 Sana
Triffst du Ali morgen?Are you meeting Ali tomorrow?
🧑 Bilal
Ja, ich treffe Ali um drei Uhr. Siehst du Ali auch?Yes, I'm meeting Ali at three o'clock. Do you see Ali too?
👧 Sana
Nein, ich sehe Ali nicht. Ich fahre nach Karachi.No, I don't see Ali. I'm driving to Karachi.

Compare ich treffe (plain stem, -e) with du triffst/sprichst (changed stem, e→i) and du siehst (e→ie) — three verbs, the same rule.

Dialog 4 — Wir essen zusammen (the full paradigm of an irregular verb in one scene)

Zara trifft Hina und ihre Freunde beim Mittagessen. (Zara meets Hina and her friends at lunch.)
🙋‍♀️ Zara
Was esst ihr?What are you (all) eating?
👋 Hina
Wir essen Biryani.We're eating biryani.
🙋‍♀️ Zara
Isst du auch, Hina?Are you eating too, Hina?
👋 Hina
Ja, ich esse auch. Und du?Yes, I'm eating too. And you?
🙋‍♀️ Zara
Ich esse auch! Wir essen alle zusammen.I'm eating too! We're all eating together.

All four forms appear here — esst (ihr), essen (wir), esse (ich), isst (du) — proof that only du and er/sie/es ever change the vowel.

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · Aussage: Subjekt + Verb (e→i) + Objekt — die du-Form (statement: subject + verb + object — the du-form)
DuSubjekt · subjectsprichstVerb · position 2, e→iDeutsch.Objekt · object, accusative

With du, sprechen's stem vowel tightens: sprechen → du sprichst. The verb still sits in position 2, exactly like any regular verb — only the vowel inside it has moved.

2 · Aussage: Subjekt + Verb (er/sie/es) + Zeit + Objekt (statement: subject + verb + time + object)
ErSubjekt · subjectisstVerb · position 2, e→ijeden TagRest · timeReis.Objekt · object, accusative

er/sie/es uses the same changed stem as du — isst, not a fresh -t stuck onto ess-. Time expressions like jeden Tag can occupy the Rest position between the verb and the object.

3 · Aussage: Subjekt (wir) + Verb (-en, unverändert) + Objekt (statement: subject + unchanged -en verb + object)
WirSubjekt · subjectsprechenVerb · position 2, -en, kein Wechsel · no changeDeutsch.Objekt · object, accusative

Swap the subject to wir and the plain vowel returns: wir sprechen, identical to the infinitive. For the stem-changing verbs taught here, only du and er/sie/es show the change — wir, ihr and sie/Sie keep the infinitive stem.

4 · Ja/Nein-Frage: Verb + Subjekt + Objekt? (yes/no question: verb + subject + object?)
SprichstVerb · position 1, e→iduSubjekt · subjectDeutsch?Objekt · object, accusative

Flipping to a yes/no question moves the verb to position 1 — but the du-form still carries its changed vowel: Sprichst du…?, never Sprechst du…?.

5 · W-Frage: W-Wort + Verb + Subjekt + Rest? (W-question: question word + verb + subject + rest?)
WasW-Wort · question wordmachstVerb · position 2duSubjekt · subjectheute?Rest · time

The W-word takes slot one, and the verb follows in position 2. machen is fully regular, so machst is just stem + -st — no vowel to worry about, unlike sprichst.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • Verbstamm bleibt, Endung wechselt: (stem stays, ending changes) With a regular verb, think of the stem as your name and the ending as your outfit, which changes with who's wearing it.
  • sprechen → du sprichst: (to speak → you speak) Talking directly to someone makes the word sharper and shorter — e tightens into i, right in your face: du sprichst.
  • essen → du/er isst: (to eat → you/he eats) Du and er eat identically — isst is the same for both, so only context tells you who's actually eating.
  • sehen → du siehst: (to see → you see) Seeing gets a two-letter spelling: e changes all the way to ie — s-ieh-st. Both vowels are long in pronunciation.
  • nehmen → du nimmst: (to take → you take) When you take something, the silent h steps out of the way and the m doubles up to grab it: nimmst.
  • fahren / schlafen → du fährst / schläfst: (to drive/sleep → you drive/sleep) Two dots (ä) land exactly on du and er, as if the umlaut is a hat only those two forms get to wear.
  • arbeiten → du arbeitest: (to work → you work) Arbeiten already ends in -t, so German slips in a friendly extra e so your tongue doesn't trip: arbeit-e-st.
  • wir / ihr / sie (Plural) / Sie → kein Vokalwechsel: (we/you all/they/formal you → no vowel change) For the stem-changing verbs here, only du and er/sie/es shift the vowel; every other person's stem matches the infinitive.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • Du sprechst gut Deutsch. → Du sprichst gut Deutsch. — sprechen changes e→i in the du-form; the infinitive's vowel does not carry over untouched.
  • Er esst jeden Tag Reis. → Er isst jeden Tag Reis. — er/sie/es uses the same changed stem as du — isst — not a fresh -t stuck onto ess-.
  • Wir sprichst Deutsch. → Wir sprechen Deutsch. — The stem-vowel change only happens in du and er/sie/es; wir always keeps the plain infinitive stem plus -en.
  • Du fahrst nach Lahore. → Du fährst nach Lahore. — fahren changes a→ä in the du-form; forgetting the umlaut is one of the most common test slips.
  • Ich arbeitst jeden Tag. → Ich arbeite jeden Tag. — ich always takes plain -e, never -st — the extra -est/-et pattern belongs to du and ihr, not ich.
  • Du heißst Ali? → Du heißt Ali? — After a stem ending in -ß, the du-form uses -t instead of -st: heiß+t = heißt.
  • Sie (formal) spielst Fußball. → Sie spielen Fußball. — The formal Sie always takes the -en ending, the same as wir and sie(plural) — never -st, which is only for informal du.
  • Ihr arbeit heute. → Ihr arbeitet heute. — Because the stem ends in -t, ihr needs the extra e before its own -t ending: arbeit+e+t.
  • Du nehmst den Bus. → Du nimmst den Bus. — nehmen doesn't just change the vowel — it also drops the h and doubles the m in the du/er forms.

Verbstruktur: Infinitiv, Konjugation & Sonderfälle (verb structure: infinitive, conjugation & special cases)

Two quiet spelling rules — one for stems ending in -s/-ß/-z, one for stems ending in -d/-t — reshape almost every du- and er/sie/es-form you'll write tomorrow. Miss them and you lose easy marks.

Die Regel (the rule)

the two spelling rules that quietly decide almost every du- and er/sie/es-form

1 · Infinitiv = Stamm + Endung (infinitive = stem + ending)

Every German infinitive breaks into two pieces: the Verbstamm (verb stem, the part that carries the meaning) and the Endung (ending, usually -en or sometimes just -n). Take lernen (to learn): stem lern- + ending -en. When you conjugate, the stem usually stays put and only the ending changes with each person: du lernst, er lernt, wir lernen.

2 · Regelmäßig (schwach) vs. unregelmäßig (stark) (regular (weak) vs. irregular (strong))

Most verbs are regelmäßig (regular), also called schwache Verben (weak verbs) — their present-tense stem stays the same no matter who is doing the action: wohnen → du wohnst, er wohnt. studieren is also regular: ich studiere, du studierst, wir studieren. Some unregelmäßige Verben (irregular verbs), including many starke Verben (strong verbs), change their stem vowel in the du- and er/sie/es-forms: sprechen → du sprichst, schlafen → du schläfst. These present-tense vowel changes have to be memorised verb by verb.

3 · Sonderfall 1: Stamm endet auf -s, -ß, -z (special case 1: stem ends in -s, -ß, -z)

Prüfungstipp: if the Verbstamm already ends in -s, -ß, or -z, German refuses to pile a second s-sound on top. The normal du-ending -st shrinks down to just -t. So reisen (stem reis-) gives du reist, never du reisst. Same with tanzen (stem tanz-) → du tanzt. This is one of the most common spots students lose easy marks — always check the last letter of the stem before adding -st.

4 · Sonderfall 2: Stamm endet auf -d oder -t (special case 2: stem ends in -d or -t)

With regular verbs whose Verbstamm ends in -d or -t, German inserts a helper vowel -e- before the du- and er/sie/es-endings so the consonants do not collide. So -st becomes -est and -t becomes -et: arbeiten (stem arbeit-) → du arbeitest, er arbeitet; antworten (stem antwort-) → du antwortest, er antwortet. Forget this rule and you'll write the unpronounceable du arbeitst — a guaranteed exam mistake.

Wortschatz: Verben nach Typ (vocabulary: verbs grouped by type)

All 14 verbs here have a neutral register.

Infinitiv-Beispiel (infinitive example — fully regular)

  • 📚lernento learn LEHR-nen · — Stamm = lern-, Endung = -en — the model verb this whole Lektion is built on.
  • 🏷️heißento be called / named HY-sen · — Stem heiß- already ends in -ß, so its du-form (du heißt) quietly follows Sonderfall 1.
  • 🚏kommento come KOM-en · — Fully regular: du kommst, er kommt — stem never changes.
  • 🛠️machento do / make MAH-khen · — Regular; same ending pattern as lernen.
  • 👂hörento hear / listen HUR-en · — Regular; du hörst, er hört.

Konjugation (conjugation — the ich-form you must never shorten)

  • 💬sagento say ZAH-gen · — Fully regular; ich-form is ich sage — never drop the final -e.

Sonderfall (special case — the two spelling rules in action)

  • ✈️reisento travel RY-zen · — Stem reis- ends in -s: du reist, not du reisst — Sonderfall 1.
  • 💃tanzento dance TAN-tsen · — Stem tanz- ends in -z: du tanzt — the -st shrinks to -t — Sonderfall 1.
  • 💼arbeitento work AR-by-ten · — Stem arbeit- ends in -t: an extra -e- appears — du arbeitest, er arbeitet — Sonderfall 2.
  • ⏳wartento wait VAR-ten · — Stem wart- ends in -t: du wartest, er wartet — Sonderfall 2.
  • ↩️antwortento answer ANT-vor-ten · — Stem antwort- ends in -t: du antwortest, er antwortet — Sonderfall 2.

Unregelmäßig: starke Verben und ein Modalverb (irregular: strong verbs and a modal verb)

  • 🗣️sprechento speak SHPREH-khen · — Stem vowel changes e→i: du sprichst, er spricht — a strong verb.
  • 🙋wollento want VOL-en · — Irregular modal verb: ich will / du willst; the irregular present-tense stem is will-.
  • 😴schlafento sleep SHLAH-fen · — Stem vowel changes a→ä: du schläfst — a strong verb.

Vier Dialoge (four dialogues using the lesson's verbs)

Dialog 1 — Der neue Schüler (the new student)
🙋‍♀️ Lena
Hallo! Ich heiße Lena. Wie heißt du?Hello! My name is Lena. What's your name?
🎒 Sara
Ich heiße Sara. Ich komme aus Pakistan.My name is Sara. I come from Pakistan.
🙋‍♀️ Lena
Sprichst du Deutsch?Do you speak German?
🎒 Sara
Ja, ich lerne Deutsch. Ich spreche ein bisschen.Yes, I'm learning German. I speak a little.
🙋‍♀️ Lena
Super! Wir lernen zusammen.Great! We'll learn together.

Notice sprechen's stem-vowel change (du sprichst / ich spreche) sitting right next to lernen, a fully regular verb — the contrast is the whole point of this Lektion.

Dialog 2 — Ferienpläne (holiday plans)
🧑 Ali
Reist du im Sommer?Are you traveling in the summer?
👩 Hina
Ja, ich reise nach Lahore. Und du?Yes, I'm traveling to Lahore. And you?
🧑 Ali
Ich arbeite im Sommer. Ich warte auf die Ferien im Winter.I work in the summer. I'm waiting for the holidays in winter.
👩 Hina
Wartest du lange?Are you waiting long?
🧑 Ali
Nein, nicht lange!No, not long!

reisen shows Sonderfall 1 (du reist), while ich arbeite and du wartest show Sonderfall 2's inserted -e- — both special cases in one short exchange.

Dialog 3 — Im Klassenzimmer (in the classroom)
👩‍🏫 Frau Klein
Was wollt ihr heute machen?What do you (all) want to do today?
🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Klasse
Wir wollen spielen!We want to play!
👩‍🏫 Frau Klein
Gut, aber zuerst arbeiten wir. Dann spielt ihr.Good, but first we work. Then you (all) play.
👦 Tom
Ich will tanzen!I want to dance!
👩‍🏫 Frau Klein
Tanzen? Nein, wir tanzen nicht in der Schule.Dance? No, we don't dance at school.

wollen's irregular ich/du-forms (ich will) sit next to its perfectly regular ihr-form (ihr wollt) and wir-form (wir wollen) — irregular verbs only break the rule in some persons, not all.

Dialog 4 — Der Anruf (the phone call)
👩 Mama
Warum antwortest du nicht?Why aren't you answering?
👦 Sam
Ich spreche mit Ali.I'm speaking with Ali.
👩 Mama
Was sagt er?What does he say?
👦 Sam
Er sagt: "Ich komme spät."He says: "I'm coming late."
👩 Mama
Okay, ich warte.Okay, I'll wait.

antwortest and warte both come from -t-stems (Sonderfall 2), while sagt shows a completely regular -t ending with no extra vowel needed — compare the two side by side.

  • 🍃die Endung / die Endungenending · the part that changes with the person: -e, -st, -t, -en

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · Aussage: Subjekt + Verb + Objekt (statement: subject + verb + object)
IchSubjekt · subjectlerneVerb · position 2Deutsch.Objekt · object

Ich lerne Deutsch. (I'm learning German.) — the plain statement order from Dialog 1: subject first and the conjugated verb in position 2.

2 · Ja/Nein-Frage: Verb + Subjekt + Objekt (yes/no question: verb + subject + object)
SprichstVerb · position 1duSubjekt · subjectDeutsch?Objekt · object

Sprichst du Deutsch? (Do you speak German?) — to ask a yes/no question, the verb moves to the front and the subject moves to position 2.

3 · W-Frage: W-Wort + Verb + Subjekt + Rest (W-question: question word + verb + subject + rest)
WasW-Wort · question wordwolltVerb · position 2ihrSubjekt · subjectheute machen?Rest + Infinitiv am Ende · rest + infinitive at the end

Was wollt ihr heute machen? (What do you all want to do today?) — the question word takes position 1, the conjugated verb stays in position 2, and the infinitive machen goes at the end.

4 · Modalverb + Infinitiv: die Satzklammer (modal verb + infinitive: the sentence bracket)
IchSubjekt · subjectwillModalverb · modal verb · position 2tanzen!Infinitiv · infinitive · Ende · end

Ich will tanzen! (I want to dance!) — wollen is conjugated in position 2 while the infinitive it needs sits at the end, bracketing the sentence as in wollen ... machen above.

5 · Verneinung: Subjekt + Verb + nicht + Rest (negation: subject + verb + not + rest)
WirSubjekt · subjecttanzenVerb · position 2nichtVerneinung · negationin der Schule.Ort · place

Wir tanzen nicht in der Schule. (We don't dance at school.) — nicht comes before the place phrase it negates here: in der Schule.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • reisen → du reist (to travel → you travel): Say "du reisst" out loud — it hisses like a snake. German hates the extra hiss, so it shaves the s away: du reist.
  • tanzen → du tanzt (to dance → you dance): The stem already ends in a "ts" sound (z). Adding -st on top would make "tantsst" — unsayable. So it drops to just -t: du tanzt.
  • arbeiten → du arbeitest (to work → you work): "Arbeitst" has two t's crashing into each other. German posts a friendly little "e" as a bridge between them: du arbeit-e-st.
  • wollen → ich will (to want → I want): Think of English "I will..." — short, no -e, no -st. Modal verbs like wollen don't play by the regular rules.
  • sprechen → du sprichst (to speak → you speak): Picture the word shrinking as you talk faster — the e in sprEchen tightens into an i: du sprIchst.
  • schlafen → du schläfst (to sleep → you sleep): A yawn stretches the a into ä — schlAfen becomes du schläfst, like the vowel is half-asleep too.
  • sagen → ich sage (to say → I say): For the full standard written form, do not let the verb go "bald": keep the -e in ich sage. The shortened ich sag' is common in conversation.
  • Verbstamm + Endung (verb stem + ending): the stem is the root of a tree (lern-); the ending is the leaves that change with the season — that is, with the person (-e, -st, -t, -en).
  • Stämme auf -d/-t brauchen ein -e- (stems ending in -d/-t need an -e-): d and t are shy consonants — in the regular verbs taught here, they need a vowel chaperone (e) before -st or -t so they don't collide: warten → wart-e-st.
  • Stämme auf -s/-ß/-z verlieren das -s aus -st (stems ending in -s/-ß/-z lose the s from -st): s, ß, and z are already hissing sounds — they don't need the s from -st tacked on again, so it vanishes: reisen → reist.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • du reisst → du reist — The stem reis- already ends in -s, so Sonderfall 1 shrinks the -st ending down to just -t.
  • du tanzst → du tanzt — The stem tanz- ends in -z; adding the full -st would be unpronounceable, so it contracts to -t.
  • du arbeitst → du arbeitest — The stem arbeit- ends in -t, so Sonderfall 2 inserts a helper -e- before -st.
  • du wartst → du wartest — Same rule as arbeiten: the stem wart- ends in -t, so the ending needs the extra -e-: wart-e-st.
  • ich sag → ich sage — In standard written German, use the full ich-form with its -e ending; the shortened ich sag' is conversational.
  • ich wille → ich will — wollen is an irregular modal verb; its ich-form is simply will, with no -e attached.
  • du sprecht → du sprichst — sprechen changes its stem vowel e→i in the du-form and takes the regular -st ending: sprichst.
  • du schlafst → du schläfst — schlafen is a starkes Verb — the stem vowel a becomes ä in the du-form.
  • er antwortt → er antwortet — The stem antwort- ends in -t, so the er/sie/es-ending -t expands to -et to stay pronounceable.
  • wir wohnt → wir wohnen — The wir-form always matches the infinitive ending -en, never the er/sie/es-ending -t.
16

Zahlen (Teil 3) & Zeit (Big Numbers & Time)

Numbers stop being two-digit friends and turn into giant one-word monsters — and the whole calendar (days, months, seasons) shows up at once. Tomorrow's test will check whether you can build 13.236 out loud and know instantly whether it's am Montag or im Januar.

Die Regel (the rule)

how German glues giant numbers into one word, reads years two different ways, and picks am or im for time

1 · Riesenzahlen sind ein Wort (giant numbers are one word)

German writes number words below one million without spaces, commas, or the word 'and'. From a few hundred up to 999.999, everything compounds into a single long word, built strictly by place value — thousands, then hundreds, then the two-digit tens-and-units pattern you already know. So 13.236 becomes dreizehntausendzweihundertsechsunddreißig — one breath, one word, no gaps. Million and Milliarde are separate nouns, as Regel 2 explains.

2 · hundert, aber eine Million (hundert, but eine Million)

hundert and tausend aren't real nouns when you're counting — they stand alone just fine (hundert or einhundert, both correct). But Million and Milliarde ARE real nouns: capitalized, pluralized normally (zwei Millionen), and always needing eine for 'one' — never just Million by itself.

3 · Jahreszahlen: vor 2000 vs. ab 2000 (years: before 2000 vs. from 2000)

Years before 2000 split into two two-digit halves joined by -hundert-: 1975 = 19 | 75 → neunzehnhundertfünfundsiebzig (exactly like English 'nineteen seventy-five'). From 2000 onward, years are read as one ordinary big number: 2017 = zweitausendsiebzehn. And to give your birth year, German uses im Jahr ... geboren: Ich bin im Jahr 2006 geboren.

4 · am oder im? Prüfungstipp! (am or im? exam tip!)

To say 'on/in' with time words, German splits the job between two prepositions. Use am (= an + dem) with days and most parts of the day: am Montag, am Morgen, am Wochenende. Use im (= in + dem) with months and seasons: im Januar, im Winter. The one exception to memorize: night takes neither — it's always in der Nacht. Prüfungstipp: if the test gives you a month or season, your automatic reflex should be im.

Wortschatz: Zahlen & Jahreszahlen (vocabulary: numbers & years)

Zahl (große Zahlen) (big numbers)

  • 💯hunderthundred HUN-dert · — No article needed for counting — just hundert; einhundert is also correct but not required.
  • 🔢tausendthousand TOW-zent · — Like hundert, tausend stands alone for counting — eintausend and tausend are both fine.
  • 💰eine Million / die Millionenone million AI-neh mil-YOHN · — Million is a real capitalized noun — it always needs eine for 'one', and becomes Millionen in the plural.
  • 🏦eine Milliarde / die Milliardenone billion AI-neh mil-YAR-deh · — Watch out — don't confuse Milliarde with Million; Milliarde has three more zeros (1,000,000,000).
  • 🔢sechshundertvierunddreißigsix hundred thirty-four (634) ZEKS-hoon-dert-feer-oont-DRY-sish · — Built in place-value order: sechshundert + vierunddreißig — hundreds first, then the familiar two-digit pattern.
  • 🧮dreizehntausendzweihundertsechsunddreißigthirteen thousand two hundred thirty-six (13.236) DRY-tsayn-tow-zent-TSVAI-hun-dert-zeks-oont-DRY-sish · /ˈdʁaɪtseːnˌtaʊzn̩tˌtsvaɪhʊndɐtˌzɛksʔʊntˈdʁaɪsɪç/ — The full method: thousands + hundreds + tens-units, glued into one word, no spaces or commas.

Jahreszahl (year numbers)

  • 🕰️neunzehnhundertfünfundsiebzignineteen seventy-five (1975) NOYN-tsayn-hun-dert-FUENF-oont-ZEEP-tsish · — Pre-2000 years split into two two-digit halves joined by -hundert-, exactly like English 'nineteen seventy-five'.
  • 📆zweitausendsiebzehntwo thousand seventeen (2017) TSVAI-tow-zent-ZEEP-tsayn · — From 2000 onward, years are read as one ordinary big number — no splitting into halves.
  • ❓Wann bist du geboren?When were you born? van bist doo geh-BOH-ren · — Formal version: Wann sind Sie geboren? — same word order, just swap du/bist for Sie/sind.
  • 🎂Ich bin im Jahr 2006 geboren.I was born in the year 2006. ikh bin im yahr TSVAI-tow-zent-zeks geh-BOH-ren · /ɪç bɪn ɪm jaːɐ̯ ˈtsvaɪtaʊzn̩tˌzɛks ɡəˈboːʁən/ — geboren goes to the very end of the sentence — German saves the last verb-piece for last.

Telefonnummer (phone number)

  • 📱die Handynummer / die Handynummernmobile/cell phone number dee HEN-dee-noo-mer · — Wie ist deine Handynummer? (informal) / Wie ist Ihre Handynummer? (formal) — same question, different pronoun.
  • 0️⃣nullzero (0) nool · — The digit you'll use constantly when reading phone numbers aloud, one digit at a time.

Wortschatz: Zeitmaß & Wochentage (vocabulary: units of time & weekdays)

Zeitmaß (unit of time)

  • ⏱️die Sekunde / die Sekundensecond dee zeh-KOON-deh · — 60 Sekunden = 1 Minute.
  • ⏲️die Minute / die Minutenminute dee mi-NOO-teh · — 60 Minuten = 1 Stunde.
  • 🕐die Stunde / die Stundenhour dee SHTOON-deh · — 24 Stunden = 1 Tag.
  • 📅der Tag / die Tageday dair tahk · — 7 Tage = 1 Woche.
  • 🗓️die Woche / die Wochenweek dee VOKH-eh · — Careful: Urdu ہفتہ can mean both 'week' and, informally, 'Saturday' — in German these are two completely different words.
  • 📆das Jahr / die Jahreyear dahs yahr · — The same word you already used in im Jahr 2006 geboren.

Wochentag (weekday)

  • 🌙der MontagMonday dair MOHN-tahk · — Named after Mond (moon) — 'moon-day', same logic as English Monday.
  • 2️⃣der DienstagTuesday dair DEENS-tahk · — All weekday names end in -tag, so once you know Tag (day) the pattern is half-learned already.
  • 3️⃣der MittwochWednesday dair MIT-vokh · — The exception to the -tag pattern — Mittwoch literally means 'mid-week', because it's the middle day.
  • ⚡der DonnerstagThursday dair DON-ers-tahk · — Named after Donner (thunder) — the same thunder-god root idea as English Thursday.
  • 5️⃣der FreitagFriday dair FRY-tahk · — Sounds close to English 'Friday' — an easy cognate to lock in.
  • 6️⃣der Samstag (auch: Sonnabend)Saturday dair ZAMS-tahk · — Sonnabend /ˈzɔnaːbənt/ (zon-AH-bent) is the same day — a regional name used more in northern/eastern Germany.
  • ☀️der SonntagSunday dair ZON-tahk · — Sonne (sun) + Tag — 'sun-day', identical logic to English.
  • 🎉das Wochenendethe weekend dahs VOKH-en-en-deh · — Neuter, not feminine like Woche — das Wochenende. Used with am: am Wochenende (on the weekend).
