Korrekturen (corrections)

  • Supermakt → Supermarkt — you wrote it without the -r- every single time, in the title and in all three sentences. Anchor it to der Markt (the market), which is sitting inside the word.
  • Enkaufskorb → Einkaufskorb — from einkaufen, so it is Ein-, not En-; the other three compounds on the page have it right.
  • Ich ben im Supermakt. → Ich bin im Supermarkt. — sein goes ich bin, du bist, er ist (Lektion 12). There is no form ben.
  • Ich Komme vom Supermakt. → Ich komme vom Supermarkt. — verbs are written small. Only nouns get a capital letter in German.
  • Ich mochhte … Kaufen. → Ich möchte … kaufen. — one h, and it needs the umlaut: möchte (Lektion 28). kaufen is a verb at the end of the sentence, so it stays lower case.
  • ein stück Käse → ein Stück Käse — the exact mirror image of the mistake above: Stück is a noun, so it goes up, while kaufen goes down.
  • Mesgenangaben → Mengenangaben — die Menge (the amount) + die Angabe (the statement), joined with an -n-. There is no s in it.
  • reciept → receipt — the English side: -ei- after the c, and the p is silent.
  • cash point → checkout / till — your English gloss for die Kasse. In British English a cash point is a cash machine, which in German is der Geldautomat — a completely different thing.
  • shopping cart → shopping trolley — the British word for der Einkaufswagen; cart is the American one, and the exam is in European German.
49

Wie ist das Wetter? (how is the weather?)

The weather words, plus the first adjective ending you have to work out for yourself (Lektion 33 only handed you der erste Juli ready-made): why your page says Es ist schön but also Es ist schönes Wetter · and the -ig suffix that turns a weather noun into a weather adjective

Wortschatz: das Wetter (vocabulary — the ten words from your page, plus the two you wrote at the bottom)

  • 🌦️das Wetter / die Wetterweather you wrote it lowercase — it is a noun, so das Wetter. The plural die Wetter is in the dictionary but you will never say it.
  • ☀️die Sonne / die Sonnensun ZON-uh · already on your alphabet page under S (Lektion 5)
  • 🌧️der Regenrain you wrote (die regen): capital R, and in real life Regen has no plural — it is a mass, like water.
  • ❄️der Schneesnow no plural either — your page was right to leave it out.
  • ⛈️das Gewitter / die Gewitterthunderstorm singular and plural look the same, like das Wetter inside it
  • 🌈der Regenbogen / die Regenbögenrainbow Regen + Bogen (arch) · der Bogen → die Bögen, so the plural takes an umlaut
  • ☁️die Wolke / die Wolkencloud -e ending → die, the rule from Lektion 19
  • ⚡der Blitz / die Blitzelightning, flash of lightning also the flash on a camera
  • 🌪️der Sturm / die Stürmestorm u → ü in the plural, like der Wunsch → die Wünsche (Lektion 30)
  • 🌬️der Wind / die Windewind you wrote der wind — capital W
  • 🌫️der Nebel / die Nebelfog you wrote der nebil — it is Nebel, with e in both syllables: NAY-bel
  • 🌤️der Himmel / die Himmelsky your page has only "Himmel → sky" with no article: it is der Himmel · am Himmel = in the sky

Eight of these twelve are der-words (Regen, Schnee, Regenbogen, Blitz, Sturm, Wind, Nebel, Himmel), two are das-words (Wetter, Gewitter) and only two are die-words (Sonne, Wolke) — weather in German leans heavily masculine. Learn each one as article + noun anyway, the way Lektion 19 told you.

Wettersätze von deiner Seite (the weather sentences from your page — corrected)

  • 🌤️Es ist schönes Wetter.It is nice weather. schön + es, because das Wetter follows with no article
  • 🌧️Es ist schlechtes Wetter.It is bad weather. the little doodle of two rainclouds sits next to this line in your Heft
  • ⛈️Es ist schreckliches Wetter.It is horrible weather. schrecklich = horrible, dreadful
  • 🙂Es ist schön.It is nice. no Wetter after it → no ending on schön
  • 😌Es ist angenehm.It is pleasant. your English said "pleasent" — the English word is pleasant
  • ☀️Es ist sonnig.It is sunny. ZON-ikh — final -ig sounds like -ich
  • 🌞Die Sonne scheint.The sun is shining. you wrote Scheint with a capital S — only the noun is capitalised
  • 🌫️Es ist neblig.It is foggy. your English said "fobgy" — the English word is foggy
  • ✨Traumhaft!Fantastic! literally "dream-like", from der Traum (dream)

Every sentence on this page except Die Sonne scheint (and the one-word exclamation Traumhaft!) uses the same frame: Es ist …. That es is not a real "it" — there is nothing it points to. German just needs something in front of the verb, because the verb must be in position 2 (Lektion 9).

Nomen → Adjektiv (the -ig suffix: turn a weather noun into a weather adjective)
Nomen (noun)Adjektiv (adjective)Satz (sentence)
die Sonnesonnig (sunny)Es ist sonnig.
der Windwindig (windy)Es ist windig.
die Wolkewolkig / bewölkt (cloudy)Es ist bewölkt.
der Nebelneblig (foggy — the -e- drops out)Es ist neblig.
der Regenregnerisch (rainy — not -ig!)Es ist regnerisch.
der Sturmstürmisch (stormy — umlaut + -isch)Es ist stürmisch.
der Schneeverschneit (snow-covered)Alles ist verschneit.
der Traumtraumhaft (fantastic)Das Wetter ist traumhaft!
Wetterverben (weather verbs — your page gives only the nouns; these are the verbs that belong to them)
VerbSatz (sentence)Perfekt (Lektion 44–46)
regnen (to rain)Es regnet.Es hat geregnet.
schneien (to snow)Es schneit.Es hat geschneit.
scheinen (to shine)Die Sonne scheint.Die Sonne hat geschienen.
wehen (to blow)Der Wind weht.Der Wind hat geweht.
blitzen (to flash)Es blitzt.Es hat geblitzt.
donnern (to thunder)Es donnert.Es hat gedonnert.
Wetterverben nehmen immer haben. (Weather verbs always take haben.) Not one of them takes sein in the Perfekt: nothing moves from A to B and nothing turns into something else, so the test you learned in Lektion 45 answers haben every single time — Es hat geregnet. Es hat geschneit. Die Sonne hat geschienen.

Fragen und Antworten (asking about the weather — not on your page, but this is the exam version of it)

  • ❓Wie ist das Wetter?How is the weather? a W-Frage (Lektion 29): W-Wort, then the verb in position 2
  • 📅Wie ist das Wetter heute?How is the weather today?
  • 🌦️Das Wetter ist heute schön.The weather is nice today. here Wetter has its article, so schön stays bare again
  • ☔Heute regnet es.It is raining today. Heute first → verb second → es third (Lektion 9)
  • 🌡️Wie viel Grad sind es heute?How many degrees is it today? answer: Es sind zwanzig Grad. — Grad stays singular after a number, like Euro in Lektion 30
  • 🌈Am Himmel ist ein Regenbogen.There is a rainbow in the sky. an + dem = am (Dativ, Lektion 32)
  • ☁️Am Himmel sind dunkle Wolken.There are dark clouds in the sky. plural, so sind — and dunkel loses its -e- before an ending: dunkle
  • 🕰️Gestern war das Wetter schlecht.Yesterday the weather was bad. war = the Präteritum from Lektion 41

Theorie (theory) · Es ist schön vs. Es ist schönes Wetter

1 · Es ist + Adjektiv — nothing follows, so nothing changes
EsSubjekt · ein Platzhalter (a placeholder)istVerb · Position 2sonnigAdjektiv · keine Endung

This is the rule you already know from Lektion 17: after sein, an adjective never changes its form. Der Himmel ist blau. Das Auto ist schnell. Es ist sonnig. One word, no ending, every time. Four of the eight sentences on your page work like this: schön · angenehm · sonnig · neblig.

2 · Es ist + Adjektiv + Nomen — now the adjective takes an ending
EsSubjektistVerb · Position 2schönesAdjektiv + -esWetterNomen · das → Neutrum

The moment the adjective stands in front of a noun, it stops being bare. das Wetter is neuter — but here there is no das in the sentence, so the adjective has to show the gender instead, and it does it with the -es borrowed from das. That is the only reason your page says schönes / schlechtes / schreckliches. Same idea as Lektion 33, where der erste Juli made the ordinal number behave like an adjective.

3 · With an article, the ending shrinks back to -e
dasArtikel · shows the gender itselfschöneAdjektiv + -eWetterNomen

Put the article back and the adjective can relax: das schöne Wetter, not das schönes Wetter. Only one of the two words has to carry the signal. You do not need the full ending table for A1 — you need this one contrast: no article → -es, article → -e.

4 · Die Sonne scheint — a real subject, a real verb
Die SonneSubjekt · NominativscheintVerb · Position 2 · klein!

The one sentence on the page that is not an Es ist … frame. scheinen = to shine. In the Präsens it is perfectly regular: die Sonne scheint, exactly the er/sie/es -t you learned in Lektion 18. (Only its Perfekt is irregular — hat geschienen, in the table above.) You wrote Scheint with a capital S; only nouns get capitals, and scheint is a verb.

5 · Wie ist das Wetter? — the question this page answers
WieW-WortistVerb · Position 2das Wetter?Subjekt · Nominativ

The W-Frage from Lektion 29, with the subject pushed behind the verb. Answer it with either frame: Es ist sonnig. or Es ist schönes Wetter. — both are complete, correct answers, and the examiner will accept either.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Adjektiv mit Endung (the adjective that carries the ending) · grey = Rest (the rest: bare adjective, noun, article) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • Why two of the plurals on your page look odd: you dutifully wrote a plural for nine of the ten nouns, and for two of them there is nothing real to write. der Regen has no plural at all in everyday German (it is a mass, like Wasser), and das Wetter has one only in weather-report language. You were right to leave der Schnee bare, and right again with der Nebel at the bottom of the page — an empty plural column is the honest answer, not a gap.
  • der Regenbogen → die Regenbögen: a compound noun always takes the gender and the plural of its last part. der Bogen → die Bögen, so der Regenbogen → die Regenbögen. This is the same rule that made das Wochenende neuter back in Lektion 16, even though die Woche is feminine.
  • The -ig ending is spoken -ich: standard German says sonnig as ZON-ikh and windig as VIN-dikh, not "-ig" as written. In the south and in Austria — and the ÖSD is an Austrian exam — you will just as often hear a hard -ik: ZON-ik. Both are accepted; say whichever comes out.
  • neblig, not nebelig: when -ig or -e is added to a word ending in -el or -er, the little e before it drops out: Nebel → neblig, dunkel → dunkle Wolken, teuer → teure. German dislikes two weak es in a row.
  • traumhaft: der Traum (dream) + -haft = "dream-like" = fantastic. It is a holiday word — exactly what you want in Lektion 47: Das Wetter im Urlaub war traumhaft. (The weather on holiday was fantastic.)
  • bei + Wetter is how Germans say "in … weather": Bei schönem Wetter gehe ich spazieren. (In nice weather I go for a walk.) The ending is -em there, not -es, because bei takes the Dativ (Lektion 32). Learn the two phrases bei schönem Wetter and bei schlechtem Wetter as fixed blocks for now.
  • Talking about yesterday's weather: two ways, both from lessons you have just done — Das Wetter war schön. (Präteritum, Lektion 41) and Gestern hat es geregnet. (Perfekt, Lektionen 44–46). For sein Germans prefer war; for the weather verbs they prefer the Perfekt.
  • Blitz and Donner come as a pair: Es blitzt und donnert. (There is lightning and thunder.) Both together, plus rain, is ein Gewitter — which is why the word contains Wetter.

Hausaufgabe (homework) · Es ist … / Es ist … Wetter

Say it in German — watch the ending on the adjective
1 · Es ist + Adjektiv (no noun after it — so no ending)
  1. It is sunny.☀️
    Es ist sonnig.die Sonne + -ig · nothing follows, so no ending
  2. It is foggy.🌫️
    Es ist neblig.der Nebel + -ig, and the -e- drops out: neblig
  3. It is windy.🌬️
    Es ist windig.der Wind + -ig
  4. It is pleasant.😌
    Es ist angenehm.angenehm = pleasant · straight off your page
2 · Es ist + Adjektiv + Wetter (a noun follows — so the adjective takes -es)
  1. It is nice weather.🌤️
    Es ist schönes Wetter.das Wetter has no article here → schön takes the -es of das
  2. It is bad weather.🌧️
    Es ist schlechtes Wetter.schlecht + es
  3. It is horrible weather.⛈️
    Es ist schreckliches Wetter.schrecklich + es
  4. The nice weather (with the article this time).📝
    das schöne Wetterthe article is back, so the adjective shrinks to -e — not schönes
3 · Ganze Sätze (full sentences)
  1. The sun is shining.🌞
    Die Sonne scheint.scheinen → sie scheint · lowercase verb
  2. It is raining.☔
    Es regnet.regnen: the stem regn- needs the full ending -et, like arbeitet in Lektion 18
  3. How is the weather today?❓
    Wie ist das Wetter heute?W-Wort first, verb second, subject third (Lektion 29)
  4. Yesterday it rained.🕰️
    Gestern hat es geregnet.Perfekt with haben; geregnet goes to the very end (Lektion 44)

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • das wetter → das Wetter — every German noun takes a capital letter; this is still the most frequent slip in the whole Heft.
  • der wind → der Wind — same rule, same page.
  • der nebil → der Nebel — the vowel is e in both syllables: NAY-bel. There is no German word Nebil.
  • Die Sonne Scheint. → Die Sonne scheint. — scheint is the verb, and verbs are never capitalised in the middle of a sentence. Only Sonne gets the capital.
  • der Regenbogen / die Regenbogen → der Regenbogen / die Regenbögen — the plural comes from der Bogen → die Bögen, so it takes the umlaut.
  • der Regen (die regen) → der Regen — kein Plural — capital R, and the plural column should simply stay empty: rain is uncountable, like snow.
  • It is pleasent. → It is pleasant. — English spelling: pleasant with an a. The German angenehm was right.
  • It is fobgy. → It is foggy. — English spelling again: foggy, no b. The German neblig was right.

trennbar (separable) means the prefix jumps to the end of the sentence. Your list has only two of them — anziehen (53) and ausziehen (54): Ich ziehe die Jacke an. (I put the jacket on.) · Er zieht die Schuhe aus. (He takes his shoes off.) Same machinery as abbiegen in Lektion 40 and anrufen in Lektion 37 — see the theory block.

Theorie (theory) · Konjugation (conjugation)

1 · Infinitive = Stamm + en
spielStamm · stem+ enEndung · ending= spielenInfinitiv · infinitive

The dictionary form of almost every verb on this page ends in -en — only lächeln (59), flüstern (62) and erinnern (68) end in a bare -n. Cut the -en off and you have the stem; every ending goes onto that stem.

2 · The six regular endings (spielen, lernen, sagen, kaufen, lachen …)
ich spiel-e-edu spiel-st-ster/sie/es spiel-t-twir spiel-en-enihr spiel-t-tsie/Sie spiel-en-en

These are the same six endings you drilled in Lektion 14. Most of the 100 verbs on this page — roughly seventy of them — need nothing more than this. wir and sie/Sie are always identical to the infinitive.

3 · Stammwechsel e → i (essen, geben, nehmen, werfen, treten, sprechen, sterben, vergessen)
ich sprechekeine Änderungdu sprichste → ier sprichte → iwir sprechenkeine Änderung

Only du and er/sie/es change; ich, wir, ihr, sie keep the e. From this page: essen → er isst · geben → er gibt · nehmen → er nimmt · werfen → er wirft · treten → er tritt · sterben → er stirbt · vergessen → er vergisst. You already met this pattern with sprechen in Lektion 14.

4 · Stammwechsel e → ie (lesen, sehen)
ich lesekeine Änderungdu lieste → ieer lieste → ieihr lestkeine Änderung

A second, longer kind of e-change: lesen → du liest, er liest and sehen → du siehst, er sieht. Note that lesen has an -s in the stem, so the du-form and the er-form come out identical: du liest = er liest.

5 · Stammwechsel a → ä (fahren, fallen, fangen, halten, tragen, waschen, schlafen) · und laufen: au → äu
ich waschekeine Änderungdu wäschsta → äer wäschta → äihr waschtkeine Änderung

Same rule, different vowel: fahren → er fährt · fallen → er fällt · fangen → er fängt · halten → er hält · tragen → er trägt · schlafen → er schläft · waschen → er wäscht. laufen stretches its au to äu: er läuft. backen (46) is optional — er backt and er bäckt are both correct; take the easy one.

6 · Kleine Schreibregeln (small spelling rules)
arbeiten → er arbeitetStamm auf -t: extra ezeichnen → er zeichnetStamm auf -chn: extra etanzen → du tanztStamm auf -z: kein extra sküssen → du küsstStamm auf -ss: kein extra s

If the stem ends in -t, -d, -chn, -ffn, an e is pushed in before the ending: er arbeitet, er wartet, er findet, er endet, er heiratet, er schneidet, er antwortet, er beobachtet, er zeichnet, er öffnet. If the stem already ends in -s, -ss, -ß, -z, the du-form just adds -t: du reist, du hasst, du küsst, du schließt, du tanzt, du putzt, du sitzt — which makes du and er/sie/es look the same. All of this is Lektion 15 (Sonderfälle) applied to a longer list.

7 · Most of these verbs take an Akkusativ object
IchSubjekt · NominativkaufeVerb · Position 2einen ApfelObjekt · Akkusativ

kaufen, verkaufen, kochen, backen, schneiden, mischen, waschen, putzen, malen, bauen, zerstören, brauchen, wählen, lieben, hassen, küssen, besuchen, vergessen, verlieren, gewinnen all act on something, and that something is the accusative object from Lektion 26 and 27: Sie kocht eine Suppe. Er backt einen Kuchen. Wir bauen ein Haus. Movement verbs (gehen, kommen, laufen, fahren, reisen, schwimmen) and position verbs (sitzen, stehen, liegen) take a place instead: Wir reisen nach Wien. Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.

8 · Trennbare Verben — anziehen und ausziehen
IchSubjekt · NominativzieheVerb · Position 2die JackeObjekt · AkkusativanPräfix · am Ende

Numbers 53 and 54 are the only separable verbs on the page. In a normal sentence the verb goes to position 2 and its prefix travels right to the end: Ich ziehe die Jacke an. Er zieht die Schuhe aus. After a modal verb they stay whole: Ich möchte die Jacke anziehen. (Lektion 28.) The same split you drew for abbiegen in Lektion 40.

9 · Verben mit Dativ — danken, antworten, glauben, gelingen
IchSubjekt · Nominativdankedanken · Verb mit DativdirDativ — nicht dich!

A handful of German verbs take their person in the Dativ, not the Akkusativ. Four of them are on your page: Ich danke dir. Ich antworte dir. Ich glaube dir. Es gelingt mir. Never Ich danke dich. Lektion 31 gave you the accusative pronouns mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie; these verbs need their dative twins instead — mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen — built on the dative case from Lektion 32. Compare fragen (93), which is the opposite: Ich frage dich. — Akkusativ.

10 · wissen — eine Information (a fact)
IchSubjekt · Nominativweißwissen · unregelmäßigdasObjekt · ein Fakt

Number 65 is irregular in the singular: ich weiß, du weißt, er weiß — the only ich-form on this page that ends in -ß with no -e. Plural is regular again: wir wissen, ihr wisst, sie wissen. Use it for facts and for whole clauses: Ich weiß, wo er wohnt.

11 · kennen — eine Person, ein Ort (a person, a place)
IchSubjekt · Nominativkennekennen · regelmäßigBerlinObjekt · Akkusativ

English has one "to know", German has two, and your page lists only wissen. kennen (ich kenne, du kennst, er kennt) means to be acquainted with a person or a place, and always takes a noun in the Akkusativ: Ich kenne seine Schwester. Ich kenne Berlin. Never Ich weiß Berlin.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ or Dativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = Präfix (separable prefix)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • drucken vs drücken — the most useful pair on the whole page: drucken (no umlaut) = to print, on paper: Ich drucke das Formular. drücken (with umlaut) = to press or squeeze: Ich drücke den Knopf. German doors say DRÜCKEN (push) and ZIEHEN (pull) — number 15 on your list. One umlaut is the whole difference.
  • gehen vs fahren vs laufen vs reisen: gehen = go on foot; fahren = go by car, bus, train, bike (Ich fahre nach Lahore.); laufen = run, but in everyday German often just "walk"; reisen = travel, for a whole journey (Wir reisen nach Österreich.).
  • bekommen is a false friend: it means to get / receive, not "to become". "To become" is werden (Lektion 28: Ich möchte Ärztin werden).
  • wachen is not "to wake up": number 56 on your page, wachen, means to keep watch / stay awake — a night guard wacht. The everyday verb you actually want is the separable aufwachen: Ich wache um sieben Uhr auf. (I wake up at seven.) Its Perfekt takes sein: Ich bin früh aufgewacht.
  • scheiden almost never stands alone: to say "they are getting divorced" German uses sich scheiden lassen: Sie lassen sich scheiden. The noun is die Scheidung (divorce), the opposite of number 87, heiraten.
  • lachen vs lächeln: lachen = to laugh out loud; lächeln = to smile. The -eln ending swallows an e in the ich-form: ich lächle, du lächelst, er lächelt. Same for flüstern (-ern): ich flüstere.
  • zeichnen vs malen: zeichnen is drawing with a pencil, lines (Er zeichnet einen Baum.); malen is painting with colour (Sie malt ein Bild.). Your page glosses 79 as "Draw" — that is right, but keep the pair apart.
  • liegen vs legen, sitzen vs setzen, stehen vs stellen: the verbs on your list describe being in a position (Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch — the book is lying on the table). Putting something into that position is a different verb (legen, setzen, stellen) — they come later.
  • treten means both "to step" and "to kick": Er tritt den Ball. · halten = hold, but also "stop" for vehicles: Der Bus hält hier. · tragen = carry, and also "wear": Sie trägt eine Tasche.
  • Prefixes that flip or intensify a meaning: kaufen → verkaufen (buy → sell), stören → zerstören (disturb → destroy), suchen → versuchen (search → try), stehen → verstehen (stand → understand). These ver-, zer-, be-, er- prefixes are untrennbar (inseparable) — they never move: Ich verstehe dich. never Ich stehe dich ver.
  • -ieren verbs are always regular: your page has one, studieren (29) — ich studiere, du studierst, er studiert, exactly as in Lektion 15. No stem change, ever. Same for telefonieren, fotografieren, buchstabieren, reparieren.
  • Capitalisation: verbs are lowercase in German (essen, trinken, drucken); your list capitalises them only because they are list headings. Inside a sentence, always lowercase — unless the verb is used as a noun, and then it is neuter: das Essen (the food/meal), das Schwimmen (swimming).
  • For the ÖSD exam: from this page the verbs you will reach for most in the speaking and writing parts are arbeiten, lernen, wohnen/leben, sprechen, lesen, schreiben, kaufen, zahlen, brauchen, warten, beginnen, spielen, besuchen, reisen, fragen, antworten and danken. Practise each one in the ich-form and the er/sie-form out loud — those are the two the examiner will hear.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • Essen, Trinken, Laufen … → in a sentence the infinitives are lowercase: essen, trinken, laufen. Capitalised, Essen is the noun (the food).
  • 22) Bekommen : recieve → bekommen : to receive — English spelling: i before e except after c.
  • 96) Gellingen → gelingen — one l. And it is a Dativ verb that only works in the 3rd person: Es gelingt mir. (I manage it / it works out for me), never Ich gelinge.
  • 97) Danken : thanks → danken : to thank — a verb, not the noun "thanks" (that is der Dank / danke!). And it takes the Dativ: Ich danke dir. · Ich danke Ihnen. — never Ich danke dich.
  • 99) Drucken : press → drucken = to print. "To press" is drücken, with an umlaut: Ich drücke den Knopf. vs Ich drucke das Foto. Learn both — this is the single most useful correction on the page.
  • 12) Liegen : lie down → liegen = to lie, to be lying (a position, not a movement). "To lie down" is sich hinlegen: Ich lege mich hin.
  • 52) Kämmen : comb (j) → kämmen = to comb; the "(j)" is a stray pen mark. Usually reflexive: Sie kämmt sich die Haare.
  • 56) Wachen : wake → wachen = to keep watch. For "to wake up" write aufwachen: Ich wache um sieben Uhr auf.
  • 88) Scheiden : divorce → normally sich scheiden lassen: Sie lassen sich scheiden. (They are getting divorced.)
  • 72) Enden : End and 79) Zeichnen : Draw → the English glosses are capitalised by accident; to end, to draw.
  • Numbers 26–100 in the earlier version of this table were a reconstruction made before your second page was photographed. They have now been replaced by your own list, verb for verb.
Ü

Übungsblatt: Nominativ, Akkusativ, Dativ (exercise sheet: the three cases)

The typed translation sheet, worked through item by item with every answer given · one drill that finally puts Lektion 19, 26 and 32 side by side, and shows you that it is the verb that decides the case

Die drei Fälle auf einen Blick (the three cases at a glance)

  • 🟢Nominativ — Wer? / Was?the subject: who or what is doing it Lektion 19 · section 1 of this sheet
  • 🟠Akkusativ — Wen? / Was?the direct object: who or what the action lands on Lektion 26 · section 2
  • 🔵Dativ — Wem?the indirect object: to or for whom, nearly always a person Lektion 32 · section 3

One single sentence on this sheet carries all three at once — item 15: Er gibt dem Kind ein Bonbon. Er = Nominativ, dem Kind = Dativ, ein Bonbon = Akkusativ. If you can see the three roles in that one line, the whole sheet opens up.

Bestimmter und unbestimmter Artikel in allen drei Fällen (the / a in all three cases — the sheet's cheat-sheet)
maskulin (der Mann)feminin (die Frau)neutral (das Kind)Plural (die Kinder)
Nominativ Wer? Was?der / eindie / einedas / eindie
Akkusativ Wen? Was?den / einendie / einedas / eindie
Dativ Wem?dem / einemder / einerdem / einemden + Nomen + n

Read the masculine column downwards: der → den → dem. That single column is where almost every mistake on this sheet happens; feminine and neuter only move in the dative row.

Theorie (theory) · Nominativ vs Akkusativ vs Dativ — one contrast, three questions

1 · Ein Satz, drei Rollen — item 15 does all three at once
ErSubjekt · Nominativ · Wer?gibtVerb · Position 2dem KindDativobjekt · Wem? · Personein BonbonAkkusativobjekt · Was? · Sache

Ask the three questions in order and the sentence sorts itself out. Wer gibt? → Er (Nominativ). Was gibt er? → ein Bonbon (Akkusativ, the thing). Wem gibt er es? → dem Kind (Dativ, the person who receives). With geben, kaufen, schenken, zeigen the person comes first and the thing second — exactly the order you learned in Lektion 32.

2 · Only the masculine article changes visibly
der MannNominativ · Wer?den MannAkkusativ · Wen?dem MannDativ · Wem?

This is why section 1 feels easy and section 3 feels hard. die Frau stays die Frau in the accusative and only becomes der Frau in the dative; das Kind stays das Kind in the accusative and becomes dem Kind in the dative. Masculine is the one that moves twice — so whenever the noun is a der-word, stop and ask which case you are in.

3 · Dativverben — helfen, danken, antworten take the Dativ, not the Akkusativ
IchSubjekt · NominativhelfeDativverb!dem MannDativ — nicht "den Mann"

This is the real teaching point of the sheet. In English "I help the man", "we thank a woman", "we answer the student" all look like plain direct objects — so your instinct writes den Mann, eine Frau, den Studenten. German disagrees: helfen, danken, antworten are Dativverben and demand dem Mann, einer Frau, dem Studenten. There is no rule to work it out from — you learn these verbs together with the word Dativ attached, the way you learn die together with Frau.

4 · Wen? oder Wem? — the trap section 5 is built around
WenAkkusativ · anrufenrufstVerb · Position 2duSubjektan?Präfix · am Ende
WemDativ · helfenhilfstVerb · Position 2du?Subjekt

English has one word, "whom", for both lines. German has two, and the verb picks. anrufen takes the accusative → Wen rufst du an?; helfen takes the dative → Wem hilfst du? Same question in English, two different German words — that is the whole reason items 3 and 4 sit next to each other on the sheet. (W-word first, verb second, subject third: Lektion 29.)

5 · mit und bei — prepositions that force the Dativ on their own
SieSubjekt · NominativwohntVerb · Position 2bei ihrer TantePräposition + Dativ

Items 16 and 17 are dative for a different reason: not the verb, but the preposition. mit, bei, aus, von, zu, nach, seit are always followed by the dative, whatever the verb is doing. So mit meinem Lehrer and bei ihrer Tante — the possessive takes the same dative ending you met in Lektion 35.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ or Dativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: preposition, place, time) · blue = W-Wort / Präfix

Hausaufgabe (homework) · 1. Nominativ — das Subjekt

Items 1–6 · translate, the subject is in the nominative
Nominativ (Wer? / Was? — nothing changes)
  1. The man is tired.😴
    Der Mann ist müde.Wer ist müde? — der Mann. The subject keeps its plain nominative article. müde = tired.
  2. A woman comes late.👩
    Eine Frau kommt spät.die Frau → eine Frau in the nominative (Lektion 20). spät = late; it is an adverb here, so no ending.
  3. The child is sick.🤒
    Das Kind ist krank.das Kind · krank = ill / sick. After ist the adjective never takes an ending (Lektion 19).
  4. The dog barks loudly.🐕
    Der Hund bellt laut.bellen is regular: er bellt. laut describes the barking, not the dog, so it stays bare — German adverbs never add -ly.
  5. A cat is sleeping.🐈
    Eine Katze schläft.schlafen is irregular, a → ä: sie schläft (Lektion 14). German has no separate "is sleeping" form — schläft covers both "sleeps" and "is sleeping".
  6. The car is new.🚗
    Das Auto ist neu.das Auto · neu = new. Section 1 asks for nothing but the plain article — this is the case you already know from Lektion 19.

Six sentences, six untouched articles. That is the point of section 1: the nominative is the form the dictionary gives you.

Hausaufgabe (homework) · 2. Akkusativ — das direkte Objekt

Items 7–12 · the action lands on the object: Wen? / Was?
Akkusativ (only masculine moves: der → den, ein → einen)
  1. I see the man.👀
    Ich sehe den Mann.Wen sehe ich? — den Mann. sehen does something to the man, so he is the direct object: der → den (Lektion 26).
  2. We met a woman.🤝
    Wir haben eine Frau getroffen.Past tense in speech = Perfekt: haben in position 2, Partizip II getroffen (treffen) at the end. Feminine eine looks identical in the accusative — nothing to change.
  3. He buys the bread.🍞
    Er kauft das Brot.das Brot is neuter, and neuter never changes in the accusative — das stays das. Do not "correct" it to dem; that would be dative.
  4. She reads a book.📖
    Sie liest ein Buch.lesen is irregular, e → ie: sie liest. Neuter ein is the same in nominative and accusative.
  5. I drink the coffee.☕
    Ich trinke den Kaffee.der Kaffee → den Kaffee — the same masculine -en you saw in item 7 and in meinen back in Lektion 27.
  6. He calls his friend.📞
    Er ruft seinen Freund an.Two things at once: anrufen is separable, so an jumps to the very end (Lektion 37); and sein → seinen because der Freund is a masculine accusative object (Lektion 27). "Er ruft seinen Freund." without the an is incomplete.

Notice how quiet this section is: four of the six answers change nothing at all. Only den Mann and den Kaffee — the two der-words — actually move.

Hausaufgabe (homework) · 3. Dativ — das indirekte Objekt

Items 13–18 · the hardest section: Wem?
Dativverben (helfen, danken, antworten — they only look like direct objects in English)
  1. I help the man.🤝
    Ich helfe dem Mann.helfen is a Dativverb. English "help the man" tempts you into den Mann, but German always says dem Mann. Learn it as one block: jemandem helfen.
  2. We thank a woman.🙏
    Wir danken einer Frau.danken is a Dativverb too, and this is the one place feminine finally moves: eine → einer (Lektion 32). Block form: jemandem danken.
  3. He gives the child a candy.🍬
    Er gibt dem Kind ein Bonbon.The true indirect object of the sheet. geben → er gibt (e → i). The receiver is Dativ (dem Kind), the thing is Akkusativ (ein Bonbon), and the person comes first. Both nouns are das-words, and they still look nothing alike here — dem against ein — because it is the case doing the work, not the gender.
  4. I talk with my teacher.🗣️
    Ich spreche mit meinem Lehrer.Dative from the preposition, not the verb: mit is always followed by the dative, so mein → meinem (Lektion 35). For a female teacher: mit meiner Lehrerin.
  5. She lives with her aunt.🏠
    Sie wohnt bei ihrer Tante."To live with someone" is bei, not mit — Sie wohnt mit ihrer Tante is simply not said in German; if you mean sharing a flat you need zusammen mit. bei also takes the dative: ihre Tante → ihrer Tante.
  6. We answer the student.🎓
    Wir antworten dem Studenten.Two traps in five words. antworten is a Dativverb → dem, not den. And der Student is an n-Deklination noun: outside the nominative it adds -en, so dem Studenten, den Studenten — never dem Student.

Three reasons for the dative live in this one section: the verb (13, 14, 18), the double object (15), and the preposition (16, 17). When you meet a dative in the exam, ask yourself which of the three it is.

Hausaufgabe (homework) · 4. möchten — would like

Items 31–36 · möchte + object in the accusative
möchten (ich möchte, du möchtest, er/sie möchte, wir möchten)
  1. I would like a tea.🍵
    Ich möchte einen Tee.What you would like is a direct object, so it is accusative: der Tee → einen Tee. The verb form is simply ich möchte (Lektion 28).
  2. He would like a pizza.🍕
    Er möchte eine Pizza.die Pizza is feminine, so eine is already the accusative form. And watch the verb: er möchte, not er möchtet — the third person singular of a modal verb adds no -t, so it looks exactly like ich möchte.
  3. We would like water.💧
    Wir möchten Wasser.wir möchten. Wasser is uncountable here, so it takes no article at all — exactly like English "would like water".
  4. She would like the cake.🍰
    Sie möchte den Kuchen."The" cake, not "a" cake — so the definite article, and der Kuchen → den Kuchen in the accusative. This item is checking that you noticed the instead of a.
  5. Would you like juice?🧃
    Möchtest du Saft?A yes/no question puts the verb in position 1 and the subject straight after it. Formally: Möchten Sie Saft? — the polite form you would actually use with a waiter (Lektion 30).
  6. We would like a table in the restaurant.🪑
    Wir möchten einen Tisch im Restaurant.der Tisch → einen Tisch (accusative, what we want). Then im = in + dem — dative, because it says where the table is, not where we are going. The same squeezing you saw with zum in Lektion 40.

Section 4 is really section 2 in disguise: after möchten everything you order is an accusative object. Only im Restaurant is dative, and that comes from the preposition.

Hausaufgabe (homework) · 5. W-Fragen — Wer, Wen, Wem, Was

Items 1–5 · the sheet is cut off after item 5
W-Wort 1 · Verb 2 · Subjekt 3 (Lektion 29)
  1. Who is the man?👤
    Wer ist der Mann?Wer asks for the subject, so it is nominative — and ist simply links two nominatives, which is why der Mann also stays der. Nothing changes anywhere in this sentence.
  2. What do you see?👀
    Was siehst du?sehen is irregular, e → ie: du siehst. German has no "do" in questions — the W-word comes first, the verb second, the subject third.
  3. Whom do you call?📞
    Wen rufst du an?anrufen takes the accusative, so the question word is Wen. The separable prefix an still goes to the very end, even in a question.
  4. Whom are you helping?🤝
    Wem hilfst du?Same English word "whom", different German word — because helfen takes the dative, so it must be Wem, never Wen. helfen is irregular too: du hilfst (e → i).
  5. What would you like?🍽️
    Was möchtest du?Was, then möchtest, then du. In a shop or a restaurant you would hear the formal version: Was möchten Sie?

Items 3 and 4 are the whole exam trap in two lines: Wen rufst du an? against Wem hilfst du? Say them out loud together until the pair sounds automatic.

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • The Dativverben worth memorising at A1: helfen (to help), danken (to thank), antworten (to answer), gehören (to belong to), gefallen (to please / to like), schmecken (to taste good), passen (to fit / suit). Three of them are on this sheet. Say them to yourself as jemandem helfen, jemandem danken, jemandem antworten — with the -em built in, you can never write the accusative by mistake.
  • n-Deklination (the "weak" masculine nouns): der Student → den / dem Studenten. The same group holds der Junge (boy), der Kollege (colleague), der Nachbar (neighbour), der Mensch (human being) and der Herr (Mr / gentleman — dem Herrn). They are all masculine people, and they all add -n or -en outside the nominative.
  • mit vs bei: Ich spreche mit meinem Lehrer. = I talk with him (together). Sie wohnt bei ihrer Tante. = She lives at her aunt's place. Both are dative, but only bei works for living somewhere — a real exam favourite.
  • möchten in full: ich möchte, du möchtest, er/sie/es möchte, wir möchten, ihr möchtet, sie/Sie möchten. Note that ich and er/sie/es are identical — no -t on the third person, which is what makes item 32 (Er möchte eine Pizza) look wrong when it is right.
  • Wer / Wen / Wem is the same der / den / dem pattern: Wer? = Nominativ (like der), Wen? = Akkusativ (like den), Wem? = Dativ (like dem). Same endings, same order. If you can say der, den, dem, you already know wer, wen, wem.
  • "We met" — why the Perfekt: in spoken German the past is normally haben/sein + Partizip II, so item 8 is Wir haben eine Frau getroffen. The helping verb sits in position 2 and the participle waits at the very end — the same bracket you built with möchten + infinitive in Lektion 28.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • What is missing from the sheet: the photographs do not show items 19–30 — they fall between section 3 (Dativ, ends at 18) and section 4 (möchten, starts at 31), and nothing above covers them. Section 5 is also cut off after item 5, so any W-question numbered 6 or higher is not here either. Everything else on the sheet is worked through above.
  • No answers were written on the sheet — it is the blank exercise, English prompts only — so there is nothing of yours to mark wrong. What follows are the six mistakes this sheet is designed to catch, written out so you can recognise them.
  • Ich helfe den Mann. → Ich helfe dem Mann. — helfen takes the Dativ.
  • Wir danken eine Frau. → Wir danken einer Frau. — danken takes the Dativ; feminine eine → einer.
  • Wir antworten dem Student. → Wir antworten dem Studenten. — n-Deklination: Student adds -en outside the nominative.
  • Sie wohnt mit ihrer Tante. → Sie wohnt bei ihrer Tante. — "to live with someone" is bei, not mit.
  • Wen hilfst du? → Wem hilfst du? — helfen is a Dativverb, so the question word must be Wem.
  • Er ruft seinen Freund. → Er ruft seinen Freund an. — anrufen is separable; the an must reach the end of the sentence.
  • Ich möchte ein Tee. → Ich möchte einen Tee. — der Tee is the accusative object of möchten.
